entries.plain_english_example: They follow the custom of avoiding matzah that has come into contact with liquid on Passover.
meanings: custom of avoiding wetted matzah on Passover
entries.context_note: A Yiddish term associated especially with Hasidic communities that avoid matzah mixed with liquid during Pesach; it is a custom, not a universal Passover prohibition.

entries.yeshivish_example: We use shmurah matzah for the Seder.
entries.plain_english_example: We use matzah made from grain guarded for the mitzvah from the required stage.
meanings: matzah produced with special supervision against becoming chametz
entries.context_note: The term refers to matzah whose grain or flour was specially guarded against leavening; practices differ as to when the guarding begins.

entries.yeshivish_example: The rav arranged the mechiras chametz before Pesach.
entries.plain_english_example: The rabbi arranged the halachic sale of chametz before Passover.
meanings: halachic transfer of ownership of chametz
entries.context_note: Used to avoid Jewish ownership of specified chametz during Pesach; practical implementation is normally arranged through a rabbi.

entries.yeshivish_example: There may be a chametz she'avar alav haPesach issue with that inventory.
entries.plain_english_example: There may be a post-Passover prohibition involving chametz that was owned by a Jew during Passover.
meanings: chametz that remained under prohibited Jewish ownership during Passover
post-Passover status of chametz owned during Pesach
entries.context_note: Relevant after Pesach when determining whether chametz was properly sold or otherwise not under prohibited Jewish ownership during the holiday.

entries.yeshivish_example: Rosh Chodesh is on Sunday and Monday this month.
entries.plain_english_example: The beginning of the new Jewish month is observed on Sunday and Monday this month.
meanings: minor festival marking the new month
entries.context_note: Can be one or two days depending on the preceding month and calendar arrangement.

entries.yeshivish_example: This Shabbos is Shabbos Mevorchim.
entries.plain_english_example: This Sabbath is the one on which the coming Jewish month is announced and blessed.
meanings: Sabbath before most new months when the coming month is blessed
entries.context_note: Usually the Shabbos before Rosh Chodesh; Tishrei is a notable exception to the ordinary practice.

entries.yeshivish_example: They announced the molad during birkas hachodesh.
entries.plain_english_example: They announced the lunar conjunction during the blessing of the new month.
meanings: prayer announcing and blessing the coming Jewish month
entries.context_note: Recited on Shabbos Mevorchim in many communities.

entries.yeshivish_example: What time is the molad?
entries.plain_english_example: What is the announced time of the lunar conjunction for the coming Jewish month?
meanings: lunar conjunction used in the Jewish calendar
announced molad time before a new month
entries.context_note: In synagogue usage, often refers to the traditional calculated molad announced before Rosh Chodesh.

entries.yeshivish_example: Which chodesh are we in now?
entries.plain_english_example: Which Jewish month are we in now?
entries.context_note: Literally “month”; often used in Yeshivish conversation for a Hebrew-calendar month.

entries.yeshivish_example: This is a shanah me'uberes, so there are two Adars.
entries.plain_english_example: This is a Jewish leap year, so there are two months of Adar.
meanings: year containing an additional month of Adar
entries.context_note: The Jewish leap year contains Adar I and Adar II.

entries.yeshivish_example: The wedding is in Adar Rishon.
entries.plain_english_example: The wedding is in the first Adar of a Jewish leap year.
meanings: first month of Adar in a Jewish leap year
entries.context_note: Also commonly called Adar I or Adar Aleph.

entries.yeshivish_example: Purim is in Adar Sheini in a leap year.
entries.plain_english_example: Purim is observed in the second Adar in a Jewish leap year.
meanings: second month of Adar in a Jewish leap year
entries.context_note: Also commonly called Adar II or Adar Beis.

entries.yeshivish_example: The event is in Nissan.
entries.plain_english_example: The event is during the Jewish month of Nissan.
entries.context_note: Jewish month containing Pesach.

entries.yeshivish_example: The event is in Iyar.
entries.plain_english_example: The event is during the Jewish month of Iyar.
entries.context_note: Jewish month following Nissan.

entries.yeshivish_example: The event is in Sivan.
entries.plain_english_example: The event is during the Jewish month of Sivan.
entries.context_note: Jewish month containing Shavuos.

entries.yeshivish_example: The event is in Tammuz.
entries.plain_english_example: The event is during the Jewish month of Tammuz.
entries.context_note: Jewish month containing the fast of the Seventeenth of Tammuz.

entries.yeshivish_example: The event is in Av.
entries.plain_english_example: The event is during the Jewish month of Av.
entries.context_note: Jewish month containing Tisha B’Av; Menachem Av is a traditional expanded name.

entries.yeshivish_example: The event is in Elul.
entries.plain_english_example: The event is during the Jewish month of Elul.
entries.context_note: Jewish month preceding Rosh Hashanah, strongly associated with repentance and preparation.

entries.yeshivish_example: The event is in Tishrei.
entries.plain_english_example: The event is during the Jewish month of Tishrei.
entries.context_note: Jewish month containing Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Sukkos, Shemini Atzeres, and Simchas Torah.

entries.yeshivish_example: The event is in Cheshvan.
entries.plain_english_example: The event is during the Jewish month of Cheshvan.
entries.context_note: Jewish month following Tishrei; also called Marcheshvan.

entries.yeshivish_example: The event is in Kislev.
entries.plain_english_example: The event is during the Jewish month of Kislev.
entries.context_note: Jewish month in which Chanukah begins.

entries.yeshivish_example: The event is in Teves.
entries.plain_english_example: The event is during the Jewish month of Teves.
entries.context_note: Jewish month containing Asarah B’Teves.

entries.yeshivish_example: The event is in Shevat.
entries.plain_english_example: The event is during the Jewish month of Shevat.
entries.context_note: Jewish month containing Tu B’Shvat.

entries.yeshivish_example: The event is in Adar.
entries.plain_english_example: The event is during the Jewish month of Adar.
entries.context_note: Jewish month containing Purim in a non-leap year.

entries.yeshivish_example: We have a lot to finish on erev Yom Tov.
entries.plain_english_example: We have a lot to finish on the day before the festival begins.
meanings: day or period immediately before a Jewish festival
entries.context_note: Often refers to the preparation day before a major Yom Tov.

entries.yeshivish_example: We are going on the trip during Chol Hamoed.
entries.plain_english_example: We are going on the trip during the intermediate festival days.
meanings: intermediate days of Pesach or Sukkos
entries.context_note: These days have festival status but fewer work restrictions than full Yom Tov.

entries.yeshivish_example: The yeshiva schedule is lighter on Isru Chag.
entries.plain_english_example: The yeshiva schedule is lighter on the day immediately after the festival.
meanings: day immediately following a pilgrimage festival
entries.context_note: A traditional name for the day after Pesach, Shavuos, or Sukkos/Shemini Atzeres.

entries.yeshivish_example: That is on Yom Tov Sheini in chutz laaretz.
entries.plain_english_example: That occurs on the second festival day observed in the Diaspora.
meanings: second festival day observed outside the Land of Israel
entries.context_note: Often shorthand for Yom Tov Sheini shel Galuyos.

entries.yeshivish_example: The second day is Yom Tov Sheini shel Galuyos.
entries.plain_english_example: The second day is the additional festival day traditionally observed in the Diaspora.
meanings: additional festival day observed in the Diaspora
entries.context_note: Applies to specified biblical festivals outside Israel; Rosh Hashanah has its own two-day structure.
entries.dialect_pattern: [Yom Tov Sheini shel Galuyos|Yom Tov Sheni shel Galuyot]

entries.yeshivish_example: Do not forget to make an eruv tavshilin before Yom Tov.
entries.plain_english_example: Do not forget the ritual preparation that permits specified cooking preparations from Yom Tov for Shabbos.
meanings: ritual food preparation made before Yom Tov when it precedes Shabbos
entries.context_note: Used when Yom Tov leads directly into Shabbos, subject to the relevant halachic rules.

entries.yeshivish_example: Gut Yom Tov!
entries.plain_english_example: Have a good festival!
entries.context_note: A general greeting for major Jewish festivals.

entries.yeshivish_example: Chag sameach!
entries.plain_english_example: Happy holiday!
entries.context_note: A general Hebrew festival greeting.

entries.yeshivish_example: Gut mo'ed!
entries.plain_english_example: Have a good intermediate-festival day!
meanings: traditional Ashkenazi greeting during Chol Hamoed
entries.context_note: Common during the intermediate days of Pesach and Sukkos.

entries.yeshivish_example: Mo'adim l'simcha!
entries.plain_english_example: May the festival times be joyous!
meanings: festival greeting commonly used during Chol Hamoed
entries.context_note: A traditional Sephardi/Israeli-style greeting especially associated with Chol Hamoed.

entries.yeshivish_example: Chagim u'zmanim l'sason!
entries.plain_english_example: May the festivals and seasons be joyful!
entries.context_note: Sometimes used in response to “mo’adim l’simcha.”

entries.yeshivish_example: Shana tova!
entries.plain_english_example: Have a good new year!
meanings: good-year greeting for Rosh Hashanah season
entries.context_note: A common Hebrew New Year greeting.

entries.yeshivish_example: Kesiva v'chasima tova!
entries.plain_english_example: May you be inscribed and sealed for a good year!
meanings: wish for favorable inscription and sealing
entries.context_note: Common before and around Rosh Hashanah in Ashkenazi/Yeshivish speech.

entries.yeshivish_example: L'shana tova tikaseiv v'seichaseim.
entries.plain_english_example: May you be inscribed and sealed for a good year.
meanings: formal traditional Rosh Hashanah greeting to a man
entries.context_note: Gendered grammatical forms vary according to the person being addressed.

entries.yeshivish_example: A gut gebentsht yor!
entries.plain_english_example: Have a good and blessed year!
entries.context_note: A traditional Yiddish greeting for the Rosh Hashanah season.

entries.yeshivish_example: Gmar chasima tova!
entries.plain_english_example: May your final sealing be for good.
meanings: traditional greeting before and on Yom Kippur
wish for a favorable final sealing
entries.context_note: Common from after Rosh Hashanah through Yom Kippur.

entries.yeshivish_example: A gut kvittel!
entries.plain_english_example: May you receive a good favorable note or verdict.
meanings: wish for a favorable final verdict
entries.context_note: A Yiddish greeting associated particularly with Hoshana Rabbah and the conclusion of the High Holiday judgment period.

entries.yeshivish_example: A lichtigen Chanukah!
entries.plain_english_example: Have a light-filled Chanukah!
meanings: Yiddish Chanukah greeting wishing a bright or light-filled holiday
entries.context_note: A traditional Yiddish-style Chanukah greeting.

entries.yeshivish_example: A freilichen Chanukah!
entries.plain_english_example: Have a joyous Chanukah!
meanings: Yiddish greeting for a happy Chanukah
entries.context_note: A common Yiddish holiday greeting.

entries.yeshivish_example: A freilichen Purim!
entries.plain_english_example: Have a joyous Purim!
entries.context_note: A common Yiddish greeting on Purim.

entries.yeshivish_example: Chag Purim sameach!
entries.plain_english_example: Happy Purim!
entries.context_note: A straightforward Hebrew greeting for Purim.

entries.yeshivish_example: A koshern un freilichen Pesach!
entries.plain_english_example: Have a kosher and joyous Passover!
entries.context_note: A common pre-Pesach and Pesach greeting emphasizing both kashrus and joy.

entries.yeshivish_example: A zissen Pesach!
entries.plain_english_example: Have a sweet Passover!
meanings: Yiddish Passover greeting wishing a sweet holiday
entries.context_note: An affectionate traditional Passover greeting.

entries.yeshivish_example: Chag Pesach kasher v'sameach!
entries.plain_english_example: Have a kosher and happy Passover!
meanings: Hebrew Passover greeting wishing a kosher and happy festival
entries.context_note: A common Hebrew Pesach greeting.

entries.yeshivish_example: Selichos starts before Rosh Hashanah.
entries.plain_english_example: The penitential prayers begin before Rosh Hashanah according to the community custom.
meanings: penitential prayers recited before and during the High Holiday season
entries.context_note: Ashkenazi communities begin Selichos before Rosh Hashanah according to calendar-based rules; additional Selichos are said on fast days.

entries.yeshivish_example: The nusach changes for the Yamim Noraim.
entries.plain_english_example: The liturgical style changes for the High Holy Days.
meanings: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur season
entries.context_note: Usually refers primarily to Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, sometimes more broadly to the surrounding season.

entries.yeshivish_example: We are staying home for Rosh Hashanah.
entries.plain_english_example: We are staying home for the Jewish New Year.
meanings: festival beginning the Ten Days of Repentance
entries.context_note: Observed on the first two days of Tishrei.

entries.yeshivish_example: People are especially careful during Aseres Yemei Teshuvah.
entries.plain_english_example: People are especially careful during the Ten Days of Repentance.
meanings: Ten Days of Repentance from Rosh Hashanah through Yom Kippur
entries.context_note: A central High Holiday period focused on repentance and judgment.

entries.yeshivish_example: The rav gives a special drasha on Shabbos Shuva.
entries.plain_english_example: The rabbi gives a special sermon on the Sabbath between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
meanings: Sabbath between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur
entries.context_note: Named for the opening word of its special prophetic reading.

entries.yeshivish_example: Did you hear shofar?
entries.plain_english_example: Did you hear the ram’s-horn blasts required on Rosh Hashanah?
meanings: ram’s horn used for ritual blasts
entries.context_note: Most strongly associated with the mitzvah of hearing shofar on Rosh Hashanah.

entries.yeshivish_example: Tekias shofar is after Krias HaTorah.
entries.plain_english_example: The shofar-blowing service is after the Torah reading.
entries.context_note: Refers to the mitzvah and structured series of Rosh Hashanah shofar blasts.

entries.yeshivish_example: The first sound is a tekiah.
entries.plain_english_example: The first shofar sound is a single sustained blast.
entries.context_note: One of the principal shofar sounds used on Rosh Hashanah.

entries.yeshivish_example: That set is tekiah-shevarim-tekiah.
entries.plain_english_example: That sequence is a sustained blast, broken blasts, and another sustained blast.
entries.context_note: One of the standard shofar sound patterns.

entries.yeshivish_example: The baal tokeia repeated the teruah.
entries.plain_english_example: The shofar blower repeated the rapid broken sound.
entries.context_note: One of the standard shofar sounds on Rosh Hashanah.

entries.yeshivish_example: The baal tokeia practiced before Yom Tov.
entries.plain_english_example: The person designated to blow the shofar practiced before the festival.
meanings: person who performs the ritual shofar blasts
entries.context_note: Common Ashkenazi term for the person blowing shofar.

entries.yeshivish_example: We are going to tashlich after the seudah.
entries.plain_english_example: We are going to the customary waterside prayer on Rosh Hashanah after the meal.
meanings: Rosh Hashanah prayer custom performed near water
entries.context_note: Traditionally performed on Rosh Hashanah, with timing variations when the first day is Shabbos or by community custom.

entries.yeshivish_example: We put the simanim on the table for the first night.
entries.plain_english_example: We put the symbolic Rosh Hashanah foods on the table for the first night.
meanings: symbolic Rosh Hashanah foods accompanied by wishes or prayers
entries.context_note: Common examples include apple and honey and other foods whose names or qualities symbolize hopes for the year.

entries.yeshivish_example: The first special section of Mussaf is malchiyos.
entries.plain_english_example: The first special Rosh Hashanah Mussaf section centers on divine kingship.
meanings: Rosh Hashanah Mussaf section about divine kingship
entries.context_note: One of the three central thematic sections of Rosh Hashanah Mussaf.

entries.yeshivish_example: Zichronos is the middle special section of Mussaf.
entries.plain_english_example: Zichronos is the middle special Rosh Hashanah Mussaf section about remembrance.
meanings: Rosh Hashanah Mussaf section about divine remembrance
entries.context_note: One of the three central thematic sections of Rosh Hashanah Mussaf.

entries.yeshivish_example: Shofros is the final special section of Mussaf.
entries.plain_english_example: Shofros is the final special Rosh Hashanah Mussaf section centered on the shofar.
meanings: Rosh Hashanah Mussaf section centered on shofar verses
entries.context_note: One of the three central thematic sections of Rosh Hashanah Mussaf.

entries.yeshivish_example: They sang Unesaneh Tokef slowly.
entries.plain_english_example: They recited the High Holiday liturgical poem Unesaneh Tokef slowly.
meanings: prominent High Holiday piyut about judgment and repentance
entries.context_note: Recited in many Ashkenazi communities during Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur Mussaf.

entries.yeshivish_example: We said Avinu Malkeinu after the Amidah.
entries.plain_english_example: We recited the “Our Father, Our King” supplications after the Amidah.
meanings: penitential prayer beginning “Our Father, Our King”
entries.context_note: Recited on many days in the High Holiday season and on certain fast days, with customs and omissions depending on the day.

entries.yeshivish_example: The shul is full on Yom Kippur.
entries.plain_english_example: The synagogue is full on the Day of Atonement.
meanings: annual fast and day of repentance on the tenth of Tishrei
entries.context_note: The culmination of the Ten Days of Repentance.

entries.yeshivish_example: We eat well on erev Yom Kippur.
entries.plain_english_example: We eat before the Yom Kippur fast begins.
entries.context_note: Associated with preparations, meals, requests for forgiveness, and other customs.

entries.yeshivish_example: They do kaparos before Yom Kippur.
entries.plain_english_example: They perform the traditional pre-Yom Kippur atonement custom.
entries.context_note: Customs vary, including the use of money or chickens.

entries.yeshivish_example: We are having the seudah hamafsekes early.
entries.plain_english_example: We are having the final meal before the fast early.
meanings: final meal before a major fast
entries.context_note: Commonly used for the pre-fast meal before Yom Kippur and Tisha B’Av, though practices differ.

entries.yeshivish_example: We got to shul before Kol Nidrei.
entries.plain_english_example: We arrived at synagogue before the opening Yom Kippur declaration concerning vows.
meanings: opening Yom Kippur declaration concerning vows
name commonly used for the opening evening service
entries.context_note: A prominent opening text of Yom Kippur evening.

entries.yeshivish_example: Yom Kippur has the chamisha inuyim.
entries.plain_english_example: Yom Kippur includes five categories of self-denial.
meanings: five forms of affliction or abstention on Yom Kippur
entries.context_note: A halachic grouping of the principal Yom Kippur restrictions beyond ordinary work prohibitions.

entries.yeshivish_example: Neilah starts late in the afternoon.
entries.plain_english_example: The concluding Yom Kippur prayer service begins late in the afternoon.
meanings: concluding prayer service of Yom Kippur
entries.context_note: The final special prayer service of Yom Kippur.

entries.yeshivish_example: We say Al Chet many times on Yom Kippur.
entries.plain_english_example: We recite the confessional litany beginning “For the sin” repeatedly on Yom Kippur.
meanings: repeated confession listing categories of sin
entries.context_note: Part of the Yom Kippur vidui liturgy.

entries.yeshivish_example: They stay in shul for Yizkor.
entries.plain_english_example: They remain in synagogue for the memorial prayer for deceased relatives.
entries.context_note: Commonly recited on Yom Kippur and on the final festival days of Pesach, Shavuos, and Shemini Atzeres according to Ashkenazi custom.

entries.yeshivish_example: We are building the sukkah for Sukkos.
entries.plain_english_example: We are building the festival booth for Sukkot.
meanings: weeklong festival beginning on the fifteenth of Tishrei
entries.context_note: A major pilgrimage festival centered on the sukkah and Four Species.

entries.yeshivish_example: We are eating in the sukkah.
entries.plain_english_example: We are eating in the temporary festival booth.
entries.context_note: A central mitzvah of Sukkos.

entries.yeshivish_example: The sechach needs to cover most of the sukkah.
entries.plain_english_example: The natural roofing material must provide the required sukkah covering.
meanings: natural roofing material of a sukkah
entries.context_note: Technical requirements govern suitable material and placement.

entries.yeshivish_example: Did you buy your arba minim yet?
entries.plain_english_example: Have you bought your Four Species for Sukkos yet?
entries.context_note: The ritual set used each day of Sukkos according to halacha, except where Shabbos rules affect practice.

entries.yeshivish_example: His lulav is very straight.
entries.plain_english_example: His palm branch for the Four Species is very straight.
meanings: palm branch used in the Four Species
sometimes shorthand for the entire Four Species set
entries.context_note: Often used colloquially for the whole assembled bundle, though technically it is the palm branch.

entries.yeshivish_example: He is checking the esrog for blemishes.
entries.plain_english_example: He is checking the citron used for Sukkos for ritual suitability.
meanings: citron used as one of the Four Species
entries.context_note: A key component of the Sukkos Four Species.

entries.yeshivish_example: The hadassim go next to the lulav.
entries.plain_english_example: The myrtle branches are bound alongside the palm branch.
meanings: myrtle branches used in the Four Species
entries.context_note: Plural of hadas; three are traditionally used in the standard set.

entries.yeshivish_example: The aravos dried out quickly.
entries.plain_english_example: The willow branches used in the Four Species dried out quickly.
meanings: willow branches used in the Four Species
willows used separately on Hoshana Rabbah
entries.context_note: Plural of aravah; relevant both to the Four Species and the Hoshana Rabbah willow custom.

entries.yeshivish_example: He did the naanuim during Hallel.
entries.plain_english_example: He performed the ritual waving of the Four Species during Hallel.
meanings: ritual waving movements of the Four Species
entries.context_note: Performed at specified points during the Sukkos prayers according to community custom.

entries.yeshivish_example: We circle the bimah during Hoshanos.
entries.plain_english_example: We circle the synagogue platform while reciting the Sukkos supplications for salvation.
meanings: Sukkos supplications recited while circling with the Four Species
entries.context_note: One circuit is customary on ordinary Sukkos days and seven on Hoshana Rabbah.

entries.yeshivish_example: Tonight we spoke about the ushpizin.
entries.plain_english_example: Tonight we discussed the traditional spiritual guests associated with the sukkah.
meanings: traditional spiritual guests of the sukkah
entries.context_note: In mystical tradition, seven biblical figures are associated with the seven days of Sukkos; some traditions add further parallel guests.

entries.yeshivish_example: There is a Simchas Beis Hashoeva tonight.
entries.plain_english_example: There is a Sukkos celebration recalling the Temple water-drawing festivities tonight.
meanings: Sukkos celebration recalling the Temple water-drawing ceremony
entries.context_note: Often marked today with music, dancing, and communal celebration.

entries.yeshivish_example: They daven early on Hoshana Rabbah.
entries.plain_english_example: They pray early on the seventh day of Sukkos.
meanings: seventh and final day of Sukkos
day with expanded Hoshanos and willow customs
entries.context_note: Carries distinctive prayers and customs and is associated in tradition with the finalization of the year’s judgment.

entries.yeshivish_example: We do chavatas aravah on Hoshana Rabbah.
entries.plain_english_example: We perform the traditional beating of willow branches on Hoshana Rabbah.
meanings: Hoshana Rabbah custom of striking willow branches
entries.context_note: A distinct custom from the aravos included in the Four Species.

entries.yeshivish_example: Yizkor is said on Shemini Atzeres.
entries.plain_english_example: The memorial prayer is recited on Shemini Atzeret.
meanings: festival immediately following the seven days of Sukkos
entries.context_note: A distinct biblical festival; in the Diaspora it is followed by Simchas Torah as a separate calendar day.

entries.yeshivish_example: We say tefillas geshem on Shemini Atzeres.
entries.plain_english_example: We recite the special prayer for rain on Shemini Atzeret.
meanings: special prayer for rain recited on Shemini Atzeres
entries.context_note: Marks the seasonal transition toward mentioning rain in the Amidah according to the liturgical calendar.

entries.yeshivish_example: The children are excited for Simchas Torah.
entries.plain_english_example: The children are excited for the festival celebrating completion and restarting of the annual Torah-reading cycle.
meanings: festival celebrating completion and renewal of the Torah-reading cycle
entries.context_note: In the Diaspora observed the day after Shemini Atzeres; in Israel the celebrations coincide with Shemini Atzeres.

entries.yeshivish_example: The second hakafah went for a long time.
entries.plain_english_example: The second celebratory circuit with the Torah scrolls lasted a long time.
meanings: circuits and dancing with Torah scrolls on Simchas Torah
entries.context_note: Commonly refers to the seven celebratory circuits on Simchas Torah and related occasions.

entries.yeshivish_example: They started Atah Hareisa before hakafos.
entries.plain_english_example: They began the verses customarily recited before the Simchas Torah circuits.
meanings: verses recited before Simchas Torah hakafos
entries.context_note: A named liturgical section preceding hakafos in many Ashkenazi rites.

entries.yeshivish_example: He received Chasan Torah this year.
entries.plain_english_example: He received the honor of the final Torah reading of the annual cycle.
meanings: person honored with the final aliyah of the Torah-reading cycle on Simchas Torah
entries.context_note: A major Simchas Torah honor.

entries.yeshivish_example: His father got Chasan Bereishis.
entries.plain_english_example: His father received the honor of the opening Torah reading from Genesis on Simchas Torah.
meanings: person honored with the first aliyah of the newly restarted Torah-reading cycle
entries.context_note: A major Simchas Torah honor following Chasan Torah.

entries.yeshivish_example: The children gathered for Kol HaNe'arim.
entries.plain_english_example: The children gathered for the special Simchas Torah aliyah associated with the children.
meanings: special Simchas Torah Torah-reading honor involving children
entries.context_note: Customs vary by community regarding how the children participate.

entries.yeshivish_example: We are going to a Chanukah party tonight.
entries.plain_english_example: We are going to a Hanukkah celebration tonight.
meanings: holiday commemorating the rededication of the Temple
entries.context_note: Begins on the twenty-fifth of Kislev and lasts eight days.

entries.yeshivish_example: Put the Chanukah menorah by the window.
entries.plain_english_example: Place the Hanukkah lamp in the appropriate visible location.
meanings: lamp used for the Chanukah lights
entries.context_note: Often simply called a menorah in English and Yeshivish conversation.

entries.yeshivish_example: The zman for ner Chanukah is coming up.
entries.plain_english_example: The time for lighting the Hanukkah lights is approaching.
meanings: mitzvah of lighting Chanukah candles or oil lamps
entries.context_note: Can refer to an individual light or to the mitzvah more generally.

entries.yeshivish_example: Hadlakas neiros Chanukah is at home tonight.
entries.plain_english_example: The Hanukkah candle-lighting is at home tonight.
entries.context_note: The nightly mitzvah performed on each of the eight nights.

entries.yeshivish_example: Use the shamash to light the other candles.
entries.plain_english_example: Use the auxiliary candle to light the other Hanukkah lights.
entries.context_note: Set apart from the principal mitzvah lights and traditionally used as a practical light source.

entries.yeshivish_example: We say Haneiros Halalu after lighting.
entries.plain_english_example: We recite the text beginning “These lights” after lighting the Hanukkah menorah.
meanings: traditional Chanukah text recited after lighting
entries.context_note: Describes the sacred commemorative purpose of the Chanukah lights.

entries.yeshivish_example: Everyone sang Maoz Tzur after lighting.
entries.plain_english_example: Everyone sang the traditional Hanukkah hymn after lighting.
entries.context_note: Commonly sung after lighting the menorah.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do not forget Al Hanissim in bentsching.
entries.plain_english_example: Do not forget the special thanksgiving insertion for Chanukah or Purim in Grace after Meals.
meanings: special thanksgiving prayer insertion for Chanukah and Purim
entries.context_note: Added to the Amidah and Birkat Hamazon on Chanukah and Purim.

entries.yeshivish_example: The window placement helps with pirsumei nisa.
entries.plain_english_example: The window placement helps publicize the miracle.
meanings: principle of making a miracle publicly known
entries.context_note: Especially associated with Chanukah lighting and also relevant to Purim practices.

entries.yeshivish_example: The kids are playing dreidel.
entries.plain_english_example: The children are playing the traditional Hanukkah spinning-top game.
entries.context_note: Yiddish-derived English/Yeshivish term for the four-sided Chanukah top.

entries.yeshivish_example: The grandparents gave the children Chanukah gelt.
entries.plain_english_example: The grandparents gave the children Hanukkah money.
entries.context_note: Gelt is Yiddish for money; Chanukah gelt may be given as real money or represented by chocolate coins.

entries.yeshivish_example: The Purim seudah is at three.
entries.plain_english_example: The Purim festive meal is at three.
meanings: festival commemorating the deliverance described in the Book of Esther
entries.context_note: Observed on the fourteenth of Adar in most places.

entries.yeshivish_example: Jerusalem observes Shushan Purim.
entries.plain_english_example: Jerusalem observes Purim on the fifteenth of Adar.
meanings: Purim observed on the fifteenth of Adar in qualifying walled cities
entries.context_note: Most prominently associated today with Jerusalem.

entries.yeshivish_example: Purim Katan is in Adar Rishon.
entries.plain_english_example: Purim Katan occurs in the first Adar of a Jewish leap year.
meanings: minor Purim observance in Adar I of a leap year
entries.context_note: The full Purim mitzvos are observed in Adar II; Purim Katan has a limited festive character.

entries.yeshivish_example: Bring a Megillas Esther to shul.
entries.plain_english_example: Bring a scroll or text of the Book of Esther to synagogue.
entries.context_note: Often simply called “the Megillah” in Purim context.

entries.yeshivish_example: Krias hamegillah is after Maariv.
entries.plain_english_example: The public reading of the Book of Esther is after the evening service.
meanings: reading of the Megillah on Purim
entries.context_note: Performed at night and during the day, subject to the laws of the mitzvah.

entries.yeshivish_example: We are packing mishloach manos.
entries.plain_english_example: We are preparing the food gifts sent to friends on Purim.
meanings: Purim gifts of ready-to-eat foods sent to another person
entries.context_note: One of the central mitzvos of Purim day.

entries.yeshivish_example: Did you give matanos l'evyonim yet?
entries.plain_english_example: Have you given the required Purim gifts to people in need yet?
meanings: charitable gifts given on Purim day
entries.context_note: One of the central mitzvos of Purim.

entries.yeshivish_example: The seudas Purim starts after Mincha.
entries.plain_english_example: The festive Purim meal begins after the afternoon prayer.
entries.context_note: A principal mitzvah of Purim day.

entries.yeshivish_example: Taanis Esther is before Purim.
entries.plain_english_example: The Fast of Esther is observed shortly before Purim.
entries.context_note: Normally observed on the thirteenth of Adar, with calendar adjustments when necessary.

entries.yeshivish_example: We give machatzis hashekel before Purim.
entries.plain_english_example: We give the customary half-shekel remembrance contribution before Purim.
meanings: half-shekel remembrance contribution associated with Purim
entries.context_note: A custom recalling the biblical half-shekel contribution; amounts and practice vary.

entries.yeshivish_example: The kids brought graggers for the Megillah.
entries.plain_english_example: The children brought noisemakers for the Purim reading.
meanings: Purim noisemaker used when Haman’s name is read
entries.context_note: A Yiddish-derived term widely used in Ashkenazi communities.

entries.yeshivish_example: He gave a funny Purim Torah at the seudah.
entries.plain_english_example: He delivered a humorous parody of Torah-style reasoning at the Purim meal.
meanings: humorous Torah parody or playful learned discourse associated with Purim
entries.context_note: Can range from harmless wordplay to elaborate parody; context signals that it is not an ordinary serious Torah teaching.

entries.yeshivish_example: It was a real venahafoch hu.
entries.plain_english_example: The situation reversed completely, like the reversal described in the Purim story.
meanings: Purim-associated phrase for a dramatic reversal
entries.context_note: From Megillas Esther; widely used figuratively in Yeshivish speech.

entries.yeshivish_example: We are going away for Pesach.
entries.plain_english_example: We are traveling for Passover.
meanings: festival commemorating the Exodus from Egypt
entries.context_note: A major pilgrimage festival beginning on the fifteenth of Nissan.

entries.yeshivish_example: Erev Pesach is always busy.
entries.plain_english_example: The day before Passover is always busy.
entries.context_note: Includes final chametz-related preparations and other distinctive laws and customs.

entries.yeshivish_example: The rav gives a long drasha on Shabbos Hagadol.
entries.plain_english_example: The rabbi gives a special sermon on the Sabbath before Passover.
entries.context_note: Traditionally associated with a major pre-Pesach sermon and distinctive customs.

entries.yeshivish_example: Bedikas chametz is after nightfall.
entries.plain_english_example: The formal search for leaven is performed after nightfall.
meanings: formal search for chametz before Pesach
entries.context_note: Usually performed on the night before Erev Pesach, with calendar adjustments when necessary.

entries.yeshivish_example: We finished biur chametz before the deadline.
entries.plain_english_example: We finished eliminating the remaining leaven before the deadline.
meanings: destruction or removal of chametz before Pesach
entries.context_note: Commonly includes burning remaining chametz on Erev Pesach.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do not forget bitul chametz after the search.
entries.plain_english_example: Do not forget the formal nullification of leaven after the search.
meanings: formal nullification of ownership or significance of chametz
entries.context_note: Recited in connection with the search and removal of chametz according to the traditional procedure.

entries.yeshivish_example: The shul is collecting maos chittim.
entries.plain_english_example: The synagogue is collecting funds to help families with Passover needs.
meanings: pre-Pesach fund for people in need
entries.context_note: Also called kimcha d’Pischa, literally “Passover flour.”

entries.yeshivish_example: Everyone needs a Haggadah at the table.
entries.plain_english_example: Everyone needs a Passover Haggadah at the Seder table.
meanings: book containing the Passover Seder text and narrative
entries.context_note: Guides the Seder and the retelling of the Exodus.

entries.yeshivish_example: Put the maror on the Seder plate.
entries.plain_english_example: Place the bitter herbs on the ritual Passover plate.
meanings: ritual plate holding symbolic Seder foods
entries.context_note: Often called the ke’arah in Hebrew/Yeshivish usage.

entries.yeshivish_example: Make sure there is enough wine for arba kosos.
entries.plain_english_example: Make sure there is enough wine for the four ritual cups at the Seder.
meanings: four cups of wine or grape juice at the Passover Seder
entries.context_note: A central rabbinic obligation of the Seder night.

entries.yeshivish_example: The youngest child is practicing Ma Nishtana.
entries.plain_english_example: The youngest child is practicing the Four Questions for the Passover Seder.
meanings: Four Questions of the Passover Seder
opening questions about why the Seder night is different
entries.context_note: Traditionally recited near the beginning of Maggid.

entries.yeshivish_example: We spent a long time on Maggid.
entries.plain_english_example: We spent a long time on the Seder section devoted to telling the Exodus story.
meanings: Seder section devoted to telling the Exodus story
entries.context_note: One of the named stages of the traditional Seder order.

entries.yeshivish_example: We dip the karpas early in the Seder.
entries.plain_english_example: We dip the vegetable used near the beginning of the Seder.
meanings: vegetable eaten near the beginning of the Seder
entries.context_note: One of the named stages and symbolic foods of the Seder.

entries.yeshivish_example: Yachatz is when we break the middle matzah.
entries.plain_english_example: Yachatz is the Seder stage when the middle matzah is broken.
meanings: Seder stage of breaking the middle matzah
entries.context_note: Part of the traditional fifteen-step Seder order.

entries.yeshivish_example: We need enough matzah for everyone.
entries.plain_english_example: We need enough unleavened bread for everyone.
entries.context_note: A central Pesach food and mitzvah; specialized forms such as shmurah matzah may have additional requirements.

entries.yeshivish_example: The horseradish is for maror.
entries.plain_english_example: The horseradish is being used for the Seder’s bitter herbs.
meanings: bitter herbs eaten at the Seder
entries.context_note: A central symbolic food recalling the bitterness of slavery.

entries.yeshivish_example: We use romaine lettuce for chazeres.
entries.plain_english_example: We use romaine lettuce for the bitter-herb component called chazeret.
meanings: one of the Seder bitter-herb items
often romaine lettuce or horseradish depending on custom and terminology
entries.context_note: Seder-plate terminology and practical identification vary by custom.

entries.yeshivish_example: The charoses is on the Seder plate.
entries.plain_english_example: The sweet paste used at the Seder is on the ritual plate.
meanings: sweet Seder paste symbolically associated with mortar
entries.context_note: Recipes vary widely by community and family custom.

entries.yeshivish_example: Korech comes after eating maror.
entries.plain_english_example: The Seder sandwich combining matzah and bitter herbs comes after maror.
meanings: Seder stage combining matzah and maror
entries.context_note: A named stage of the traditional Seder order.

entries.yeshivish_example: The children hid the afikoman.
entries.plain_english_example: The children hid the piece of matzah reserved for the end of the Seder meal.
meanings: piece of matzah eaten near the end of the Seder
Seder matzah often hidden for children as a custom
entries.context_note: The required eating at the end of the meal commemorates the Pesach offering in the traditional Seder framework.

entries.yeshivish_example: The zeroa goes on the Seder plate.
entries.plain_english_example: The roasted shank-bone or substitute goes on the Seder plate.
meanings: Seder plate item recalling the Passover offering
entries.context_note: Customs differ regarding the exact item used and whether it is eaten.

entries.yeshivish_example: The beitzah goes on the Seder plate.
entries.plain_english_example: The roasted egg goes on the Seder plate.
meanings: roasted egg on the Seder plate
entries.context_note: Traditionally associated with the festival offering and mourning symbolism in different explanations.

entries.yeshivish_example: The kids stayed awake for Chad Gadya.
entries.plain_english_example: The children stayed awake for the cumulative song at the end of the Haggadah.
meanings: traditional cumulative song at the end of the Passover Seder
entries.context_note: A well-known closing song of the Haggadah.

entries.yeshivish_example: Everyone joined in for Echad Mi Yodea.
entries.plain_english_example: Everyone joined the numbered question-and-answer song near the end of the Seder.
meanings: traditional numbered song at the end of the Haggadah
entries.context_note: A familiar closing song of the Seder.

entries.yeshivish_example: Today is Pesach Sheini.
entries.plain_english_example: Today is the minor date known as the Second Passover.
meanings: Second Passover on the fourteenth of Iyar
date recalling the biblical makeup opportunity for the Passover offering
entries.context_note: Today often marked by customs such as eating matzah in some communities.

entries.yeshivish_example: What night of Sefiras HaOmer is it?
entries.plain_english_example: Which night of the Counting of the Omer is it?
meanings: forty-nine-day count from Pesach to Shavuos
entries.context_note: The count begins on the second night of Pesach and culminates before Shavuos.

entries.yeshivish_example: We are in the middle of the Omer.
entries.plain_english_example: We are in the period of counting between Passover and Shavuos.
meanings: Omer-counting period between Pesach and Shavuos
biblical measure and offering underlying the count
entries.context_note: In ordinary Yeshivish conversation “the Omer” often means the Sefirah period.

entries.yeshivish_example: There is a bonfire on Lag BaOmer.
entries.plain_english_example: There is a celebration on the thirty-third day of the Omer count.
entries.context_note: Associated with Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and with a relaxation of some mourning practices according to community custom.

entries.yeshivish_example: We stay up learning on Shavuos night.
entries.plain_english_example: We stay awake studying Torah on the night of Shavuot.
meanings: festival commemorating the giving of the Torah
entries.context_note: A major pilgrimage festival observed fifty days from the start of the Omer count.

entries.yeshivish_example: They are learning Tikkun Leil Shavuos all night.
entries.plain_english_example: They are following the traditional all-night Shavuot study program.
meanings: traditional Shavuos-night study text or all-night study practice
entries.context_note: Many communities stay awake studying Torah on the first night of Shavuos; exact study material varies.

entries.yeshivish_example: Shavuos is zman matan Toraseinu.
entries.plain_english_example: Shavuot commemorates the giving of the Torah.
meanings: giving of the Torah at Sinai
entries.context_note: A central theme of Shavuos.

entries.yeshivish_example: In davening we call Shavuos zman matan Toraseinu.
entries.plain_english_example: In the festival liturgy Shavuot is called the season of the giving of our Torah.
meanings: liturgical description of Shavuos as the season of the giving of the Torah
entries.context_note: A standard phrase in the Shavuos festival Amidah and Kiddush.

entries.yeshivish_example: The shul is crowded for Aseres Hadibros.
entries.plain_english_example: The synagogue is crowded for the Torah reading of the Ten Commandments.
meanings: Decalogue read in the Torah on Shavuos
entries.context_note: Also appears in other Torah-reading contexts, but strongly associated with Shavuos morning.

entries.yeshivish_example: They sing Akdamus before the Torah reading.
entries.plain_english_example: They chant the traditional Aramaic Shavuot poem in connection with the Torah reading.
meanings: Aramaic liturgical poem recited on Shavuos in many Ashkenazi communities
entries.context_note: Custom and placement vary by rite.

entries.yeshivish_example: They learn Megillas Rus on Shavuos.
entries.plain_english_example: They study or read the Book of Ruth on Shavuot.
meanings: Book of Ruth traditionally associated with Shavuos
entries.context_note: Public reading customs vary among communities.

entries.yeshivish_example: Shavuos is connected with bringing bikkurim.
entries.plain_english_example: Shavuot is associated with the biblical bringing of first fruits to the Temple.
meanings: first fruits brought to the Temple
biblical offering strongly associated with Shavuos
entries.context_note: A major biblical theme of Shavuos and agricultural festival terminology.

entries.yeshivish_example: Tomorrow is a taanis.
entries.plain_english_example: Tomorrow is a Jewish fast day.
entries.context_note: Can refer to an individual fast or a public fast day.

entries.yeshivish_example: It has the halachos of a taanis tzibbur.
entries.plain_english_example: It has the laws and prayers of a communal fast.
entries.context_note: Public fasts have distinctive prayer additions and Torah readings according to halacha.

entries.yeshivish_example: Shiva Asar b'Tammuz begins the Three Weeks.
entries.plain_english_example: The Fast of the Seventeenth of Tammuz begins the Three Weeks mourning period.
meanings: Fast of the Seventeenth of Tammuz
entries.context_note: A public fast commemorating calamities connected with the destruction of Jerusalem.

entries.yeshivish_example: Those restrictions apply during the Three Weeks.
entries.plain_english_example: Those mourning practices apply during the three-week period leading up to Tisha B’Av.
meanings: mourning period from the Seventeenth of Tammuz through Tisha B’Av
entries.context_note: Called Bein Hametzarim in Hebrew; specific practices vary by community and stage of the period.

entries.yeshivish_example: Those restrictions apply during Bein Hametzarim.
entries.plain_english_example: Those mourning practices apply during the period known as the Three Weeks.
meanings: period between the fast of 17 Tammuz and Tisha B’Av
entries.context_note: Hebrew name for the summer mourning period preceding Tisha B’Av.

entries.yeshivish_example: We do not eat meat during the Nine Days.
entries.plain_english_example: According to common Ashkenazi practice, additional mourning restrictions apply during the first nine days of Av.
meanings: period from Rosh Chodesh Av through Tisha B’Av with intensified mourning customs
entries.context_note: Exact practices vary by community and circumstance.

entries.yeshivish_example: Tisha B'Av is a full fast.
entries.plain_english_example: Tisha B’Av is a major fast commemorating the destruction of the Temples and other calamities.
meanings: fast of the Ninth of Av
entries.context_note: Marked by fasting, mourning practices, Eicha, and Kinos.

entries.yeshivish_example: They read Eicha after Maariv.
entries.plain_english_example: They read the Book of Lamentations after the evening prayer on Tisha B’Av.
meanings: public reading on Tisha B’Av night
entries.context_note: Traditionally read in a mournful chant.

entries.yeshivish_example: Kinos takes most of the morning.
entries.plain_english_example: The elegies recited on Tisha B’Av occupy much of the morning.
entries.context_note: Also recited in some other mourning contexts, but most commonly refers to the Tisha B’Av collection.

entries.yeshivish_example: This week is Shabbos Chazon.
entries.plain_english_example: This week is the Sabbath immediately preceding Tisha B’Av.
entries.context_note: Named for its prophetic reading beginning with “Chazon.”

entries.yeshivish_example: Shabbos Nachamu is after Tisha B'Av.
entries.plain_english_example: The Sabbath of consolation follows Tisha B’Av.
entries.context_note: Named for its prophetic reading beginning with “Nachamu.”

entries.yeshivish_example: Tzom Gedaliah is right after Rosh Hashanah.
entries.plain_english_example: The Fast of Gedaliah is observed immediately after Rosh Hashanah.
meanings: Fast of Gedaliah on the third of Tishrei, with calendar adjustments
entries.context_note: A public fast during the Ten Days of Repentance.

entries.yeshivish_example: Asarah B'Teves is a winter fast.
entries.plain_english_example: The Tenth of Tevet is a public fast day in the winter.
meanings: Fast of the Tenth of Teves
entries.context_note: Commemorates the beginning of the siege of Jerusalem leading to the destruction of the First Temple.

entries.yeshivish_example: Tu B'Shvat is the New Year for trees.
entries.plain_english_example: The fifteenth of Shevat is the traditional New Year for trees.
meanings: minor Jewish calendar date on the fifteenth of Shevat
entries.context_note: Often marked by eating fruits, especially produce associated with the Land of Israel.

entries.yeshivish_example: Tu B'Av is considered a joyous day.
entries.plain_english_example: The fifteenth of Av is traditionally considered a joyous date.
meanings: minor festive date on the fifteenth of Av
entries.context_note: Historically associated with matchmaking and other joyous events.

entries.yeshivish_example: This week is Parshas Shekalim.
entries.plain_english_example: This week includes the special Torah reading about the half-shekel.
meanings: first of the four special Torah readings before Pesach
entries.context_note: Read around Rosh Chodesh Adar according to the calendar.

entries.yeshivish_example: Everyone makes sure to hear Parshas Zachor.
entries.plain_english_example: Everyone makes sure to hear the special Torah reading about remembering Amalek.
meanings: special Torah reading before Purim about remembering Amalek
entries.context_note: One of the four special pre-Pesach Torah readings and closely associated with Purim.

entries.yeshivish_example: Parshas Parah is coming up.
entries.plain_english_example: The special Torah reading about the red heifer is approaching.
meanings: special Torah reading about the red heifer before Pesach
entries.context_note: One of the four special Torah readings in the weeks leading to Pesach.

entries.yeshivish_example: Parshas Hachodesh is before Nissan or on Rosh Chodesh Nissan.
entries.plain_english_example: The special Torah reading about the new month is read before or on the beginning of Nissan.
meanings: special Torah reading introducing Nissan and Pesach preparations
entries.context_note: One of the four special Torah readings before Pesach.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do not forget Yaaleh Veyavo tonight.
entries.plain_english_example: Do not forget the special Rosh Chodesh or festival insertion in the Amidah and Grace after Meals.
meanings: special prayer insertion for Rosh Chodesh and festivals
entries.context_note: Recited in the Amidah and Birkat Hamazon on Rosh Chodesh and festival days according to the calendar.

entries.yeshivish_example: The Yom Tov Amidah begins its central blessing with Atah Vechartanu.
entries.plain_english_example: The central festival blessing of the Amidah begins with the words “You chose us.”
meanings: central festival Amidah paragraph beginning “You chose us”
entries.context_note: A standard defining text of the Yom Tov Amidah.

entries.yeshivish_example: We say tefillas tal on the first day of Pesach.
entries.plain_english_example: We recite the seasonal prayer for dew on the first day of Passover.
entries.context_note: Recited at the seasonal transition on Pesach according to the rite.

entries.yeshivish_example: We start saying mashiv haruach umorid hageshem on Shemini Atzeres.
entries.plain_english_example: We begin mentioning wind and rain in the Amidah at the seasonal transition on Shemini Atzeret.
meanings: seasonal Amidah phrase mentioning wind and rain
entries.context_note: Introduced during the Shemini Atzeres rain-season liturgy and omitted at the corresponding spring transition; pronunciation customs vary.

entries.yeshivish_example: Some nuschaos say morid hatal in the summer.
entries.plain_english_example: Some prayer rites mention dew in the Amidah during the summer season.
entries.context_note: Use depends on nusach and season.

entries.yeshivish_example: We have not started v'sein tal umatar here yet.
entries.plain_english_example: We have not yet begun the seasonal request for dew and rain in the weekday Amidah here.
meanings: seasonal request for dew and rain in the weekday Amidah
entries.context_note: The start date differs between the Land of Israel and the Diaspora and follows halachic calendar rules.

entries.yeshivish_example: Chodesh tov!
entries.plain_english_example: Have a good new month!
meanings: Hebrew greeting for Rosh Chodesh or the new Jewish month
entries.context_note: A common greeting around Rosh Chodesh.

entries.yeshivish_example: A gutten chodesh!
entries.plain_english_example: Have a good new month!
meanings: Yiddish greeting for Rosh Chodesh or the new Jewish month
entries.context_note: The Yiddish counterpart of “Chodesh tov.”

entries.yeshivish_example: We will make Havdalah after Yom Tov.
entries.plain_english_example: We will perform the ritual marking the transition from sacred time to ordinary time after the festival.
meanings: ritual marking the end of Shabbos or Yom Tov
separation ceremony over wine and prescribed blessings
entries.context_note: The exact form differs depending on whether Shabbos, Yom Tov, or another sacred day is ending and what follows.

entries.yeshivish_example: Tonight the Kiddush follows yaknehaz.
entries.plain_english_example: Tonight the festival Kiddush includes the special sequence used when Yom Tov begins on Saturday night.
meanings: acronym for the Kiddush-Havdalah sequence when Yom Tov begins on Saturday night
entries.context_note: Represents the ordered elements of wine, Kiddush, flame, Havdalah, and Shehecheyanu in the relevant situation.

entries.yeshivish_example: Hadlakas neiros is before Yom Tov begins.
entries.plain_english_example: Festival candle lighting takes place at the appropriate time before or during the festival according to the calendar and custom.
meanings: lighting Shabbos or Yom Tov candles
ritual candle lighting before sacred days
entries.context_note: Timing and method vary between Shabbos, Yom Tov, and cases when one sacred day follows another.

entries.yeshivish_example: The milah is scheduled for this morning.
entries.plain_english_example: The circumcision ceremony is scheduled for this morning.
meanings: the circumcision component of the covenant ceremony
entries.context_note: Often appears as part of the phrase bris milah. The base glossary already contains bris as the broader ceremony.

entries.yeshivish_example: The mohel will arrive before the bris.
entries.plain_english_example: The person trained to perform the ritual circumcision will arrive before the ceremony.
entries.context_note: A mohel is the person who performs a Jewish ritual circumcision.

entries.yeshivish_example: His grandfather will be the sandek.
entries.plain_english_example: His grandfather will hold the baby in the honored role during the circumcision.
meanings: honored person who holds the baby during the bris
entries.context_note: A major honor at a bris, traditionally associated with holding the baby during the circumcision.

entries.yeshivish_example: They asked him to be the kvatter at the bris.
entries.plain_english_example: They asked him to help carry the baby into the circumcision ceremony.
meanings: person participating in carrying the baby into the bris
entries.context_note: A Yiddish term for a person given the honor of conveying the baby into the bris ceremony; details of the role vary by custom.

entries.yeshivish_example: She was honored as the kvatterin.
entries.plain_english_example: She was honored to participate in bringing the baby into the circumcision ceremony.
meanings: woman participating in carrying the baby into the bris
entries.context_note: The feminine Yiddish form corresponding to kvatter; exact ceremonial roles vary by community.

entries.yeshivish_example: We are going to the shalom zachar Friday night.
entries.plain_english_example: We are going to the traditional gathering held on the first Friday night after a baby boy is born.
meanings: Friday-night gathering after the birth of a baby boy
entries.context_note: An Ashkenazi custom held on the first Friday night after the birth of a boy.

entries.yeshivish_example: The children came to say Shema at the vach nacht.
entries.plain_english_example: The children came for the traditional gathering on the night before the circumcision.
entries.context_note: A custom observed in some Ashkenazi communities on the night before a bris; practices vary by community.

entries.yeshivish_example: The baby was brought near the kisei shel Eliyahu.
entries.plain_english_example: The baby was brought near the special chair associated with Elijah at the circumcision ceremony.
meanings: chair of Elijah used at a bris
entries.context_note: A special chair associated with Eliyahu Hanavi at a bris.

entries.yeshivish_example: They invited us to the seudas bris.
entries.plain_english_example: They invited us to the festive meal following the circumcision.
entries.context_note: The celebratory meal associated with a bris.

entries.yeshivish_example: The pidyon haben is next week.
entries.plain_english_example: The redemption ceremony for the firstborn son is next week.
entries.context_note: A mitzvah performed for a qualifying firstborn son, in which the father redeems him from a kohen.

entries.yeshivish_example: He is the bechor in the family.
entries.plain_english_example: He is the firstborn son in the family.
entries.context_note: The halachic category of firstborn has specific definitions; in ordinary conversation the word commonly means firstborn.

entries.yeshivish_example: Pidyon haben applies only when the child meets the rules of peter rechem.
entries.plain_english_example: The redemption applies only when the child qualifies as the first issue of the womb under Jewish law.
meanings: halachic firstborn status relevant to pidyon haben
entries.context_note: A technical halachic term used in determining eligibility for pidyon haben.

entries.yeshivish_example: They brought five selaim to the kohen for the pidyon haben.
entries.plain_english_example: They brought the redemption payment to a man of priestly lineage for the firstborn ceremony.
meanings: priest, especially a descendant of Aaron
entries.context_note: A kohen has special roles and restrictions in Jewish law. In this lifecycle section the term is especially relevant to pidyon haben and mourning laws.

entries.yeshivish_example: The father gave the kohen chamisha selaim.
entries.plain_english_example: The father gave the kohen the prescribed five-sela redemption value.
meanings: five selaim used for pidyon haben
entries.context_note: The Torah-prescribed redemption amount for pidyon haben; practical valuation of the silver is a halachic matter.

entries.yeshivish_example: They are making a simchas bas on Sunday.
entries.plain_english_example: They are holding a celebration for the birth and naming of their daughter on Sunday.
entries.context_note: A general term used for a celebration connected with the birth or naming of a girl; customs vary.

entries.yeshivish_example: The krias shem will be during the Torah reading.
entries.plain_english_example: The baby will be formally given her Jewish name during the Torah reading.
meanings: giving or announcing a Jewish name
entries.context_note: Literally calling a name; used for formally giving or announcing a Jewish name.

entries.yeshivish_example: His upsherin will be on his third birthday.
entries.plain_english_example: His traditional first haircut celebration will be on his third birthday.
meanings: traditional first haircut ceremony for a young boy
entries.context_note: A custom in many communities, commonly held around a boy’s third birthday. The Hebrew/Sephardic term chalakah is included as a variant.

entries.yeshivish_example: They left his peyos at the upsherin.
entries.plain_english_example: They left the side-lock areas of his hair uncut at the first haircut ceremony.
meanings: hair at the sides of the head governed by the prohibition against rounding the corners
entries.context_note: Commonly discussed at an upsherin and in everyday Orthodox dress and grooming.

entries.yeshivish_example: She does shadchanus for several families.
entries.plain_english_example: She works at suggesting and facilitating marriage matches for several families.
entries.context_note: The activity or field of matchmaking.

entries.yeshivish_example: They paid the shadchanus gelt after the engagement.
entries.plain_english_example: They paid the customary matchmaking fee after the engagement.
entries.context_note: A Yeshivish/Yiddish expression for payment made to a matchmaker.

entries.yeshivish_example: Who redt this shidduch?
entries.plain_english_example: Who suggested or arranged this marriage match?
meanings: suggest or propose a marriage match
act as the person who brings a shidduch idea
entries.context_note: A Yiddish-derived phrase used in Yeshivish English. Spelling and conjugation vary widely.

entries.yeshivish_example: They met at a beshow before the families continued the shidduch.
entries.plain_english_example: They met at a formal arranged meeting used in some communities before proceeding with the match.
meanings: formal prospective-marriage meeting in some Hasidic communities
entries.context_note: A community-specific shidduch term, especially in some Hasidic circles; not universal Yeshivish usage.

entries.yeshivish_example: The families signed the tenoyim before the wedding.
entries.plain_english_example: The families formalized the engagement arrangements before the wedding.
meanings: ceremony or document associated with an engagement
entries.context_note: Historically a formal set of marriage conditions; in contemporary communities it may refer to an engagement ceremony or document, with practices varying.

entries.yeshivish_example: They made a kinyan when the agreement was finalized.
entries.plain_english_example: They performed a formal Jewish-law act of acquisition to give legal effect to the agreement.
meanings: legal mechanism for creating an obligation or transfer
entries.context_note: A broad halachic concept used in many legal contexts, including marriage-related documents and agreements.

entries.yeshivish_example: They are expecting a baby, so we wished them b'shaah tovah.
entries.plain_english_example: They are expecting a baby, so we wished that everything happen at the proper and favorable time.
meanings: a traditional wish used before a future happy event
entries.context_note: Often used for pregnancy and other anticipated milestones where speakers may avoid congratulating before the event occurs. Usage varies by community.

entries.yeshivish_example: Besoroes tovos; keep us posted.
entries.plain_english_example: May we hear good news; keep us posted.
entries.context_note: A common wish when awaiting an outcome, recovery, birth, match, or other hoped-for development.

entries.yeshivish_example: His aufruf is this Shabbos.
entries.plain_english_example: He will be called to the Torah in the traditional pre-wedding celebration this Sabbath.
meanings: pre-wedding Torah aliyah for a groom
entries.context_note: An Ashkenazi custom in which the groom is called to the Torah, commonly on the Shabbos before the wedding.

entries.yeshivish_example: Her friends are coming for the Shabbos kallah.
entries.plain_english_example: Her friends are gathering with the bride on the Sabbath before the wedding.
meanings: pre-wedding Sabbath gathering for a bride
entries.context_note: A pre-wedding custom whose form varies by community.

entries.yeshivish_example: The kabbalas panim starts an hour before the chuppah.
entries.plain_english_example: The pre-wedding reception begins an hour before the wedding canopy ceremony.
entries.context_note: At an Orthodox wedding, often refers to the separate pre-chuppah receptions for the groom and bride.

entries.yeshivish_example: The witnesses signed documents at the chosson tish.
entries.plain_english_example: The witnesses handled pre-wedding formalities at the groom’s table gathering.
entries.context_note: A Yiddish/Hebrew hybrid term for the groom’s pre-wedding gathering; customs and formalities vary.

entries.yeshivish_example: Everyone gathered for the badeken before the chuppah.
entries.plain_english_example: Everyone gathered for the ceremony in which the groom veils the bride before the wedding canopy.
entries.context_note: A Yiddish term meaning covering or veiling, used for the traditional ceremony before the chuppah.

entries.yeshivish_example: The chuppah is called for six o’clock.
entries.plain_english_example: The wedding-canopy ceremony is scheduled for six o’clock.
meanings: marriage ceremony held beneath the canopy
entries.context_note: Can refer to the physical canopy or, conversationally, to the central wedding ceremony.

entries.yeshivish_example: The rav will be the mesader kiddushin.
entries.plain_english_example: The rabbi will officiate and oversee the Jewish marriage ceremony.
meanings: rabbi or authority who officiates at kiddushin
person arranging the halachic marriage ceremony
entries.context_note: The officiating rabbinic role responsible for properly arranging the marriage ceremony.

entries.yeshivish_example: The ring is given as part of the kiddushin.
entries.plain_english_example: The ring is given as part of the halachic betrothal stage of marriage.
meanings: first legal stage of Jewish marriage
entries.context_note: In the contemporary wedding ceremony, kiddushin and nisuin are performed together even though they are conceptually distinct stages.

entries.yeshivish_example: The first bracha is connected with erusin.
entries.plain_english_example: The first marriage blessing relates to the betrothal stage.
meanings: legal engagement stage, often equivalent to kiddushin in halachic usage
entries.context_note: In classical halachic terminology, erusin is the betrothal stage; it is not identical to a modern social engagement.

entries.yeshivish_example: The chuppah completes the nisuin stage.
entries.plain_english_example: The wedding canopy completes the full-marriage stage of the ceremony.
meanings: completion of the marriage stage following kiddushin
entries.context_note: The second legal stage of Jewish marriage, following kiddushin/erusin.

entries.yeshivish_example: The mesader kiddushin recited birkas erusin over the wine.
entries.plain_english_example: The officiant recited the blessing associated with the betrothal stage over wine.
entries.context_note: The blessing recited at the beginning of the halachic marriage ceremony.

entries.yeshivish_example: The eidim signed the kesubah before the chuppah.
entries.plain_english_example: The witnesses signed the Jewish marriage contract before the ceremony.
entries.context_note: A formal Aramaic marriage document setting out the husband’s obligations and the financial protections due to the wife.

entries.yeshivish_example: He was asked to serve as an eid for the kiddushin.
entries.plain_english_example: He was asked to serve as a halachic witness to the marriage.
entries.context_note: Singular of eidim. Jewish-law witness qualifications depend on the legal context.

entries.yeshivish_example: The eidim watched the ring being given.
entries.plain_english_example: The witnesses observed the act that effects the marriage.
entries.context_note: Plural of eid; marriage requires properly qualified witnesses.

entries.yeshivish_example: He said harei at mekudeshes li when giving the ring.
entries.plain_english_example: He recited the traditional declaration of betrothal while giving the ring.
meanings: you are hereby betrothed to me
opening words of the traditional kiddushin declaration
entries.context_note: A recognizable portion of the formula used when effecting kiddushin. This glossary entry identifies the phrase rather than providing legal instructions.

entries.yeshivish_example: The chosson and kallah went to yichud after the chuppah.
entries.plain_english_example: The bride and groom went to a private room together after the wedding ceremony.
meanings: private time of the bride and groom following the ceremony
entries.context_note: At Ashkenazi Orthodox weddings, commonly refers to the private room entered by the newly married couple after the chuppah.

entries.yeshivish_example: We are invited to sheva brachos tonight.
entries.plain_english_example: We are invited to a newlywed celebration at which the seven marriage blessings may be recited.
meanings: post-wedding meal or celebration during the first week
entries.context_note: Can mean the seven blessings themselves or a meal during the post-wedding week at which they are recited when the requirements are met.

entries.yeshivish_example: They are still in the sheva yemei hamishteh.
entries.plain_english_example: They are still within the seven-day wedding celebration period.
entries.context_note: The seven-day celebratory period beginning with the wedding; practical laws depend on circumstances.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do we have panim chadashos for sheva brachos tonight?
entries.plain_english_example: Is there a qualifying new guest for tonight’s seven-blessings meal?
meanings: qualifying new participant for certain sheva-brachos meals
entries.context_note: A technical condition relevant to reciting sheva brachos at meals during the wedding week; details vary by halachic circumstance.

entries.yeshivish_example: They are observing the taanis chosson v'kallah until the chuppah.
entries.plain_english_example: The bride and groom are observing the traditional wedding-day fast until the ceremony.
meanings: wedding-day fast of bride and groom
entries.context_note: A custom in many Ashkenazi communities; exceptions and practices vary.

entries.yeshivish_example: Shviras hakos comes at the end of the chuppah.
entries.plain_english_example: Breaking the glass comes near the end of the wedding ceremony.
meanings: breaking the glass at a Jewish wedding
entries.context_note: A customary act at the conclusion of the chuppah, commonly associated with remembrance of the destruction of Jerusalem.

entries.yeshivish_example: The broken glass is done as a zecher l'churban.
entries.plain_english_example: The broken glass is done as a remembrance of the destruction of the Temple.
meanings: practice commemorating the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple
entries.context_note: A broad phrase used for customs that preserve remembrance of the Churban, including wedding practices.

entries.yeshivish_example: The mitzvah tantz was held late at the wedding.
entries.plain_english_example: The traditional ceremonial dance was held late in the wedding celebration.
meanings: ceremonial wedding dance in some Hasidic communities
entries.context_note: A Hasidic wedding custom and not universal across Yeshivish or Orthodox communities.

entries.yeshivish_example: The badchan introduced the honors with rhyming verses.
entries.plain_english_example: The traditional wedding entertainer or master of ceremonies introduced the honors with rhyming verses.
entries.context_note: Especially associated with traditional or Hasidic weddings; exact role varies.

entries.yeshivish_example: Everyone sang siman tov u'mazel tov after the chuppah.
entries.plain_english_example: Everyone sang a traditional wish for a good sign and congratulations after the wedding ceremony.
meanings: a good sign and good fortune
traditional celebratory wedding or lifecycle refrain
entries.context_note: A standard celebratory phrase and song used at weddings and other happy lifecycle events. The base glossary separately contains mazel tov.

entries.yeshivish_example: The band started od yishama as the dancing began.
entries.plain_english_example: The band began the traditional wedding song based on the verse about voices of joy being heard again.
meanings: opening words of a traditional Jewish wedding verse and song
entries.context_note: A common shorthand for the wedding verse/song beginning with the words “od yishama.”

entries.yeshivish_example: We wished them a bayis ne'eman b'Yisrael.
entries.plain_english_example: We wished them a faithful and enduring Jewish home.
meanings: traditional blessing for a newly married couple
entries.context_note: A common wedding blessing expressing hope that the couple build a stable Jewish home.

entries.yeshivish_example: May their marriage be a binyan adei ad.
entries.plain_english_example: May their marriage be an enduring union.
entries.context_note: A poetic wedding blessing comparing marriage to an enduring structure.

entries.yeshivish_example: They are still in shana rishona.
entries.plain_english_example: They are still in their first year of marriage.
entries.context_note: In Yeshivish conversation, often specifically refers to a couple’s first year of marriage.

entries.yeshivish_example: They are working on shalom bayis.
entries.plain_english_example: They are working on peace and harmony in their marriage and home.
entries.context_note: Often used specifically for healthy relations between spouses, though literally it means peace in the household.

entries.yeshivish_example: Her baal is learning in the next room.
entries.plain_english_example: Her husband is studying in the next room.
meanings: owner or master in other contexts
entries.context_note: In Yeshivish usage baal can mean husband, but the Hebrew word has several other meanings and requires context.

entries.yeshivish_example: The sugya discusses the status of an eishes ish.
entries.plain_english_example: The Talmudic discussion addresses the status of a married woman.
meanings: woman legally married under Jewish law
entries.context_note: A halachic status term, not merely a conversational synonym for wife.

entries.yeshivish_example: The beis din handles matters of gerushin.
entries.plain_english_example: The rabbinical court handles matters of Jewish divorce.
entries.context_note: The general Hebrew term for divorce, especially in halachic discussion.

entries.yeshivish_example: She received the get through the beis din.
entries.plain_english_example: She received the Jewish bill of divorce through the rabbinical court.
entries.context_note: A properly written and delivered get is central to Jewish divorce law. This glossary entry is descriptive, not procedural.

entries.yeshivish_example: They went to a rav who is experienced as a mesader get.
entries.plain_english_example: They went to a rabbi experienced in arranging a Jewish divorce.
meanings: rabbinic authority who arranges a get
entries.context_note: A specialized role requiring expertise in Jewish divorce law.

entries.yeshivish_example: The matter was brought to a beis din.
entries.plain_english_example: The matter was brought before a rabbinical court.
entries.context_note: A court of dayanim that adjudicates matters under Jewish law; scope and authority depend on context.

entries.yeshivish_example: A dayan reviewed the documents.
entries.plain_english_example: A rabbinical judge reviewed the documents.
entries.context_note: A rabbinic judge qualified to decide matters of Jewish law.

entries.yeshivish_example: The organization helps an agunah obtain a get.
entries.plain_english_example: The organization helps a woman unable to obtain the Jewish divorce needed to remarry under Jewish law.
meanings: woman unable to remarry because her Jewish marriage remains unresolved
entries.context_note: A sensitive halachic and social status. The exact legal situation can arise for more than one reason.

entries.yeshivish_example: The case also involved the status of an agun.
entries.plain_english_example: The case also involved a man whose marital status was halachically unresolved.
meanings: man whose marital status is unresolved or who cannot remarry in a relevant halachic circumstance
entries.context_note: The masculine counterpart term is less common in everyday English than agunah.

entries.yeshivish_example: The beis din issued instructions concerning a mesarev get.
entries.plain_english_example: The rabbinical court addressed a person refusing to cooperate with giving or receiving a required Jewish divorce.
entries.context_note: A sensitive legal label whose proper application depends on the specific beis-din ruling and circumstances.

entries.yeshivish_example: The rav said that a heter meah rabbanim is an exceptional procedure.
entries.plain_english_example: The rabbi said that permission involving one hundred rabbis is an exceptional Jewish-law procedure.
meanings: special dispensation involving one hundred rabbis
entries.context_note: A rare and technical Ashkenazi halachic mechanism with significant procedural requirements.

entries.yeshivish_example: The masechta discusses yibum and chalitzah.
entries.plain_english_example: The tractate discusses levirate marriage and the ceremony that releases the parties from it.
meanings: marriage of a childless widow to her deceased husband’s brother under Torah law
entries.context_note: A technical Torah-law institution whose modern practical treatment depends on community and halachic tradition.

entries.yeshivish_example: They needed a beis din for chalitzah.
entries.plain_english_example: They needed a rabbinical court for the ceremony releasing the widow and brother-in-law from the levirate bond.
meanings: ceremony releasing a widow and brother-in-law from yibum
entries.context_note: A formal halachic ceremony related to yibum.

entries.yeshivish_example: The halacha discusses the obligations of the yavam.
entries.plain_english_example: Jewish law discusses the status of the deceased husband’s brother in a yibum case.
meanings: brother-in-law subject to yibum or chalitzah
entries.context_note: Technical family-law term.
