entries.yeshivish_example: The mishnah discusses the yevamah before chalitzah.
entries.plain_english_example: The Mishnah discusses the widow subject to yibum or chalitzah.
meanings: widow subject to yibum or chalitzah
entries.context_note: Technical family-law term.

entries.yeshivish_example: The halacha has specific rules concerning an almana.
entries.plain_english_example: Jewish law has specific rules concerning a widow.
entries.context_note: Common Hebrew/halachic term for a widow.

entries.yeshivish_example: He became an alman several years ago.
entries.plain_english_example: He became a widower several years ago.
entries.context_note: Hebrew term for a widower; less frequent in Yeshivish English than almana.

entries.yeshivish_example: The discussion concerns the status of a gerusha.
entries.plain_english_example: The discussion concerns the status of a divorced woman.
entries.context_note: A legal-status term with particular relevance in some areas of Jewish law.

entries.yeshivish_example: The term mamzer has a very specific halachic meaning.
entries.plain_english_example: The term refers to a narrowly defined Jewish-law lineage status, not simply to an illegitimate child.
meanings: specific prohibited-lineage status under Jewish law
entries.context_note: A sensitive and frequently mistranslated halachic status; it should not be rendered simply as “bastard” or “illegitimate child.”

entries.yeshivish_example: The same lineage rules can apply to a mamzeres.
entries.plain_english_example: The same narrowly defined lineage status can apply to a woman.
meanings: female person with the halachic status of mamzer
entries.context_note: Feminine form of mamzer; a sensitive technical status.

entries.yeshivish_example: We heard about his petirah this morning.
entries.plain_english_example: We heard about his passing this morning.
entries.context_note: A common respectful Hebrew/Yeshivish term for a person’s death.

entries.yeshivish_example: The niftar was well known in the community.
entries.plain_english_example: The deceased man was well known in the community.
entries.context_note: Masculine term commonly used respectfully for the deceased.

entries.yeshivish_example: The nifteres taught for many years.
entries.plain_english_example: The deceased woman taught for many years.
entries.context_note: Feminine counterpart of niftar.

entries.yeshivish_example: The halacha discusses kavod hameis.
entries.plain_english_example: Jewish law discusses the honor due to the deceased.
meanings: corpse or deceased person in halachic terminology
entries.context_note: A direct halachic term that can sound clinical in ordinary English; respectful speech often uses niftar/nifteres instead.

entries.yeshivish_example: The sugya discusses what happens after meisah.
entries.plain_english_example: The Talmudic discussion addresses what happens after death.
entries.context_note: A halachic/textual term for death; not the usual condolence expression.

entries.yeshivish_example: The levaya will leave the shul at noon.
entries.plain_english_example: The funeral procession will leave the synagogue at noon.
meanings: funeral procession or accompanying the deceased
entries.context_note: Literally accompanying; commonly means the funeral or procession accompanying the deceased to burial.

entries.yeshivish_example: Levayas hameis is considered a major chesed.
entries.plain_english_example: Accompanying the deceased to burial is considered an important act of kindness.
entries.context_note: The mitzvah or act of accompanying the deceased, broader than merely attending a funeral service.

entries.yeshivish_example: The kevurah took place that afternoon.
entries.plain_english_example: The burial took place that afternoon.
entries.context_note: The act of burying the deceased.

entries.yeshivish_example: They went to the kever on the yahrzeit.
entries.plain_english_example: They visited the grave on the anniversary of the death.
entries.context_note: Common Hebrew/Yeshivish term for a grave.

entries.yeshivish_example: The levaya continued to the beis hachaim.
entries.plain_english_example: The funeral continued to the Jewish cemetery.
meanings: Jewish cemetery, literally house of life
entries.context_note: A traditional euphemistic name for a cemetery.

entries.yeshivish_example: They purchased a plot in the beis olam.
entries.plain_english_example: They purchased a burial plot in the cemetery.
entries.context_note: Another traditional Hebrew term for a cemetery.

entries.yeshivish_example: The chevra kadisha arranged the taharah and burial.
entries.plain_english_example: The Jewish burial society arranged the ritual preparation and burial.
meanings: group responsible for care of the deceased and burial
entries.context_note: Literally holy society; commonly the organization or volunteers handling traditional Jewish burial preparations.

entries.yeshivish_example: Serving on the chevra kadisha is called a chesed shel emes.
entries.plain_english_example: Caring for the deceased is described as a kindness that cannot be repaid by the recipient.
entries.context_note: Often applied to burial and funeral care because the deceased cannot repay the favor.

entries.yeshivish_example: They changed the schedule because of kavod hameis.
entries.plain_english_example: They changed the schedule to preserve the dignity and honor of the deceased.
meanings: dignity owed to a dead person
entries.context_note: A central principle affecting treatment, transport, burial, and other decisions concerning the deceased.

entries.yeshivish_example: The chevra kadisha performed taharas hameis.
entries.plain_english_example: The burial society performed the traditional ritual preparation and purification of the deceased.
meanings: ritual preparation and purification of the deceased before burial
entries.context_note: This phrase distinguishes burial taharah from family-purity uses of the word taharah.

entries.yeshivish_example: They arranged shmira until the levaya.
entries.plain_english_example: They arranged for the deceased not to be left unattended before the funeral.
meanings: guarding or attending the body before burial
entries.context_note: Traditional practice of maintaining a watch over the deceased until burial.

entries.yeshivish_example: A shomer hameis stayed there overnight.
entries.plain_english_example: A person assigned to watch over the deceased remained there overnight.
meanings: person who watches over the deceased before burial
entries.context_note: The person performing shmira.

entries.yeshivish_example: The niftar was dressed in tachrichim.
entries.plain_english_example: The deceased was dressed in traditional Jewish burial shrouds.
entries.context_note: Traditional Jewish burial garments.

entries.yeshivish_example: The aron was carried to the graveside.
entries.plain_english_example: The coffin was carried to the graveside.
meanings: casket; also means cabinet or ark in other contexts
entries.context_note: In burial context aron means coffin or casket; in synagogue context the same word can mean the Torah ark, so context is essential.

entries.yeshivish_example: The rav discussed whether the delay creates a problem of halanas hameis.
entries.plain_english_example: The rabbi discussed whether delaying the burial overnight raises a Jewish-law concern.
entries.context_note: A technical burial-law concept with exceptions and details that require halachic guidance.

entries.yeshivish_example: The Gemara discusses the special obligations of a meis mitzvah.
entries.plain_english_example: The Talmud discusses the special duty to bury an unattended deceased person.
meanings: deceased person with no one available to arrange burial
entries.context_note: A technical halachic category carrying unusually strong burial obligations.

entries.yeshivish_example: A kohen has to be careful about tumas meis.
entries.plain_english_example: A kohen must be careful about ritual impurity associated with contact or proximity to the dead.
meanings: ritual impurity associated with a corpse
entries.context_note: A technical ritual-purity category especially relevant to kohanim and burial settings.

entries.yeshivish_example: The rosh yeshiva gave a hesped at the levaya.
entries.plain_english_example: The head of the yeshiva delivered a eulogy at the funeral.
meanings: formal words of mourning and praise for the deceased
entries.context_note: A funeral or memorial eulogy, usually focused on the deceased’s life and loss.

entries.yeshivish_example: He was asked to be maspid at the levaya.
entries.plain_english_example: He was asked to deliver a eulogy at the funeral.
entries.context_note: The person who gives a hesped.

entries.yeshivish_example: They recited El Malei Rachamim at the memorial.
entries.plain_english_example: They recited the traditional memorial prayer asking for divine mercy for the deceased.
meanings: Jewish memorial prayer for the deceased
entries.context_note: A memorial prayer commonly recited at funerals, memorial occasions, and cemetery visits in many Ashkenazi communities.

entries.yeshivish_example: During aninus, the immediate family has a distinct halachic status.
entries.plain_english_example: Before burial, immediate mourners have a distinct Jewish-law status with special rules.
meanings: period between death and burial for an immediate mourner
entries.context_note: A technical status applying to specified close relatives before burial; practical rules require halachic guidance.

entries.yeshivish_example: He was an onen until the kevurah.
entries.plain_english_example: He had the special pre-burial status of an immediate mourner until burial.
entries.context_note: Masculine person-form corresponding to aninus.

entries.yeshivish_example: She was an onenes until the burial.
entries.plain_english_example: She had the special pre-burial status of an immediate mourner until burial.
entries.context_note: Feminine person-form corresponding to aninus.

entries.yeshivish_example: He is still in aveilus for a parent.
entries.plain_english_example: He is still observing the Jewish mourning period for a parent.
meanings: halachic state and practices of bereavement
entries.context_note: The general term for Jewish mourning observance after burial.

entries.yeshivish_example: The avel is saying Kaddish.
entries.plain_english_example: The mourner is reciting Kaddish.
entries.context_note: Singular masculine/general form for a mourner.

entries.yeshivish_example: Neighbors brought food for the aveilim.
entries.plain_english_example: Neighbors brought food for the mourners.
entries.context_note: Plural of avel.

entries.yeshivish_example: They are sitting shiva at the family home.
entries.plain_english_example: They are observing the seven-day mourning period at the family home.
entries.context_note: The intensive seven-day mourning period counted from burial, subject to rules concerning holidays and other circumstances.

entries.yeshivish_example: Minyan will be at the beis avel.
entries.plain_english_example: The prayer quorum will meet at the house of mourning.
meanings: home where shiva is being observed
entries.context_note: Often the location where visitors come for nichum aveilim and where prayer services are held during shiva.

entries.yeshivish_example: The family is still within shloshim.
entries.plain_english_example: The family is still within the thirty-day mourning period.
meanings: first thirty days from burial including shiva
entries.context_note: The thirty-day mourning period counted from burial; restrictions differ by relationship to the deceased and other circumstances.

entries.yeshivish_example: For a parent, some aveilus continues through yud beis chodesh.
entries.plain_english_example: For a parent, aspects of mourning continue through the twelve-month period.
meanings: twelve-month mourning period for a parent
entries.context_note: A common Yeshivish shorthand for the extended mourning period for a parent.

entries.yeshivish_example: The aveilim made keriah before the burial.
entries.plain_english_example: The mourners tore a garment as required in the mourning ritual.
entries.context_note: A formal mourning act performed by specified mourners, generally around the funeral or burial depending on custom.

entries.yeshivish_example: We went for nichum aveilim after work.
entries.plain_english_example: We went to comfort the mourners after work.
entries.context_note: The mitzvah of comforting mourners, commonly performed by visiting during shiva.

entries.yeshivish_example: We went to be menachem avel.
entries.plain_english_example: We went to comfort the mourner.
meanings: person or act of consoling a mourner, depending on construction
entries.context_note: Commonly appears in the phrase “to be menachem avel,” meaning to pay a condolence visit.

entries.yeshivish_example: Neighbors prepared the seudas havraah after the kevurah.
entries.plain_english_example: Neighbors prepared the traditional first meal for the mourners after burial.
meanings: first meal provided to mourners after the funeral
entries.context_note: The first meal eaten by mourners after burial, traditionally provided by others.

entries.yeshivish_example: His yahrzeit is next week.
entries.plain_english_example: The annual Jewish-calendar anniversary of his death is next week.
entries.context_note: A Yiddish term for the annual anniversary of a person’s death, observed according to the Jewish calendar.

entries.yeshivish_example: The family marked the yom hashanah with learning and tzedakah.
entries.plain_english_example: The family marked the anniversary of the death with Torah study and charity.
entries.context_note: Literally anniversary; in mourning context it can refer to the yahrzeit.

entries.yeshivish_example: She lit a yahrzeit candle before nightfall.
entries.plain_english_example: She lit a memorial candle for the anniversary of the death.
meanings: memorial candle lit for a yahrzeit
entries.context_note: A candle or light traditionally kindled for a yahrzeit and certain memorial occasions.

entries.yeshivish_example: They lit a ner neshama in his memory.
entries.plain_english_example: They lit a memorial light in memory of the deceased.
entries.context_note: A Hebrew term for a memorial light, often used for yahrzeit or other remembrance.

entries.yeshivish_example: The family visited the matzeivah.
entries.plain_english_example: The family visited the gravestone.
entries.context_note: Commonly means the headstone or monument marking a Jewish grave.

entries.yeshivish_example: The hakamas matzeivah will be after shloshim.
entries.plain_english_example: The dedication or setting of the gravestone will take place after the thirty-day period.
meanings: setting or dedication of a gravestone
entries.context_note: Communities differ on timing and ceremony; sometimes described in English as an unveiling.

entries.yeshivish_example: The shiur was sponsored l'ilui nishmas his father.
entries.plain_english_example: The Torah class was sponsored for the spiritual elevation of his father’s soul.
meanings: for the elevation of the soul of
in memory of, with spiritual merit intended for the deceased
entries.context_note: Common dedication phrase before the name of a deceased person.

entries.yeshivish_example: They learned Mishnayos for an aliyas neshama.
entries.plain_english_example: They studied in the hope of bringing spiritual elevation to the deceased soul.
meanings: spiritual ascent or merit for the deceased
entries.context_note: Used when discussing mitzvos, Torah learning, or charity performed in memory of the deceased.

entries.yeshivish_example: May the neshama have an aliyah.
entries.plain_english_example: May the soul experience spiritual elevation.
entries.context_note: A broad religious term; in mourning conversation it often specifically means the soul of the deceased.

entries.yeshivish_example: Baruch Dayan Ha'emes; we just heard the news.
entries.plain_english_example: Blessed is the true Judge; we just heard the news of the death.
meanings: traditional response or blessing upon hearing of a death
entries.context_note: A traditional Jewish response to news of a death. The exact blessing with God’s name has halachic rules; conversational use often omits the divine-name formula.

entries.term: Hamakom yenachem eschem b'soch sha'ar aveilei Tzion v'Yerushalayim
entries.aleph_beis: המקום ינחם אתכם בתוך שאר אבלי ציון וירושלים
entries.yeshivish_example: Before leaving, he said Hamakom yenachem eschem.
entries.plain_english_example: Before leaving, he recited the traditional Ashkenazi words of comfort to the mourners.
meanings: may God comfort you among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem
entries.context_note: A standard Ashkenazi condolence formula used during shiva. Gender and singular/plural forms can vary.

entries.yeshivish_example: Rabbi Cohen, zichrono livracha, taught here for decades.
entries.plain_english_example: Rabbi Cohen, of blessed memory, taught here for decades.
meanings: may his memory be a blessing
entries.context_note: A respectful phrase after the name of a deceased man; often abbreviated z”l.

entries.yeshivish_example: Mrs. Cohen, zichrona livracha, founded the program.
entries.plain_english_example: Mrs. Cohen, of blessed memory, founded the program.
meanings: may her memory be a blessing
entries.context_note: Feminine form of zichrono livracha.

entries.yeshivish_example: The sefer quotes Rav Moshe, zecher tzaddik livracha.
entries.plain_english_example: The book quotes Rav Moshe, may the memory of the righteous be a blessing.
meanings: may the memory of the righteous be a blessing
honorific for a deceased righteous person
entries.context_note: A reverential phrase often used after the name of a deceased rabbinic or righteous figure; commonly abbreviated zt”l.

entries.yeshivish_example: His father, alav hashalom, was a longtime gabbai.
entries.plain_english_example: His late father, may he rest in peace, was a longtime synagogue official.
meanings: respectful phrase for a deceased man
entries.context_note: A traditional phrase appended to the name or reference to a deceased man; often abbreviated a”h.

entries.yeshivish_example: Her mother, aleha hashalom, was known for her chesed.
entries.plain_english_example: Her late mother, may she rest in peace, was known for her kindness.
meanings: respectful phrase for a deceased woman
entries.context_note: Feminine counterpart of alav hashalom.

entries.yeshivish_example: His name was followed by Hashem yikom damo.
entries.plain_english_example: His name was followed by the traditional phrase asking God to avenge his blood.
meanings: honorific used for a Jew killed through violence or persecution
entries.context_note: Traditionally used for someone killed because of anti-Jewish violence or persecution; application should follow community convention and context.

entries.yeshivish_example: They mentioned the rebbe, zechuso yagen aleinu.
entries.plain_english_example: They referred to the deceased righteous leader with the phrase “may his merit protect us.”
meanings: reverential phrase for a deceased righteous person
entries.context_note: Common after names of revered deceased rabbis or tzaddikim; frequently abbreviated זיע״א.

entries.yeshivish_example: The inscription ends with tehei nishmaso tzrurah b'tzror hachayim.
entries.plain_english_example: The inscription ends with the traditional wish that his soul be bound in the bond of life.
meanings: may his soul be bound in the bond of life
entries.context_note: A traditional memorial phrase commonly represented on gravestones by the Hebrew abbreviation תנצב״ה; feminine grammar may differ depending on the person.

entries.yeshivish_example: Please accept our tanchumim.
entries.plain_english_example: Please accept our condolences.
entries.context_note: General Hebrew term for condolences or consolation after a loss.

entries.yeshivish_example: Rachmana litzlan, there was a terrible accident.
entries.plain_english_example: May the Merciful One spare us; there was a terrible accident.
meanings: may the Merciful One save us
entries.context_note: An Aramaic expression used when mentioning tragedy, danger, or something deeply undesirable. It is broader than mourning but common in that context.

entries.yeshivish_example: I left the sefer in the beis midrash.
entries.plain_english_example: I left the religious book in the study hall.
meanings: Torah book or sacred Jewish text
entries.context_note: In Yeshivish, sefer commonly means a Jewish religious book rather than any book.

entries.yeshivish_example: The new shelves are for sefarim.
entries.plain_english_example: The new shelves are for religious books.
entries.context_note: Plural of sefer; often used collectively for a home or synagogue Torah library.

entries.yeshivish_example: Please do not put food on the sifrei kodesh.
entries.plain_english_example: Please do not put food on the sacred books.
entries.context_note: A general term for Jewish religious texts that are treated with respect.

entries.yeshivish_example: Take a chumash so you can follow the leining.
entries.plain_english_example: Take a printed Torah volume so you can follow the public reading.
meanings: printed volume of the Five Books of Moses
Pentateuch used for study or following the Torah reading
entries.context_note: Often contains the Torah text together with commentaries and sometimes the haftaros.

entries.yeshivish_example: The pasuk is in Tanach.
entries.plain_english_example: The verse is in the Hebrew Bible.
entries.context_note: An acronym for Torah, Neviim, and Kesuvim.

entries.yeshivish_example: That haftorah comes from Nevi'im.
entries.plain_english_example: That prophetic reading comes from the Prophets.
meanings: Prophets section of the Hebrew Bible
entries.context_note: The second major division of Tanach.

entries.yeshivish_example: Tehillim is part of Kesuvim.
entries.plain_english_example: Psalms is part of the Writings.
meanings: Writings section of the Hebrew Bible
entries.context_note: The third major division of Tanach.

entries.yeshivish_example: We learned that Mishnah yesterday.
entries.plain_english_example: We studied that unit of the Mishnah yesterday.
entries.context_note: Can mean the work as a whole or an individual unit of Mishnah.

entries.yeshivish_example: They divided the Mishnayos among the family.
entries.plain_english_example: They divided the Mishnah study among the family.
entries.context_note: Commonly used for studying chapters or tractates of Mishnah, including in memorial learning.

entries.yeshivish_example: Which masechta are they learning this zman?
entries.plain_english_example: Which Talmudic tractate are they studying this term?
entries.context_note: In yeshiva conversation, usually a tractate being learned.

entries.yeshivish_example: What daf are you holding on?
entries.plain_english_example: Which Talmud folio are you up to?
entries.context_note: In Gemara study, daf normally refers to a folio with an a and b side.

entries.yeshivish_example: He goes to a daf yomi shiur every morning.
entries.plain_english_example: He attends a daily Talmud-cycle class every morning.
entries.context_note: A worldwide study schedule completing the Babylonian Talmud in a fixed cycle.

entries.yeshivish_example: We finished the perek.
entries.plain_english_example: We finished the chapter.
entries.context_note: Commonly used for chapters of Tanach, Mishnah, or other Torah texts.

entries.yeshivish_example: Look in siman shin yud ches.
entries.plain_english_example: Look in the numbered legal section indicated.
meanings: numbered section in a halachic work
entries.context_note: Especially common in Shulchan Aruch and later halachic works.

entries.yeshivish_example: The din is in se'if beis.
entries.plain_english_example: The rule is in subsection two.
entries.context_note: A subdivision of a siman in works such as Shulchan Aruch.

entries.yeshivish_example: See se'if katan five.
entries.plain_english_example: See subcomment five.
entries.context_note: Often used when citing commentaries such as Mishnah Berurah.

entries.yeshivish_example: Can you send me the mareh makom?
entries.plain_english_example: Can you send me the source reference?
entries.context_note: Literally a place-reference; often means the source for a statement.

entries.yeshivish_example: The rebbe gave out mareh mekomos.
entries.plain_english_example: The teacher distributed a source-reference sheet.
meanings: source sheet or list of references
entries.context_note: Often used for a prepared sheet of sources for a shiur or chavrusa.

entries.yeshivish_example: The Shulchan Aruch discusses the case.
entries.plain_english_example: The Code of Jewish Law discusses the case.
entries.context_note: Commonly cited simply by title in practical halachic discussion.

entries.yeshivish_example: Check the Mishnah Berurah on that siman.
entries.plain_english_example: Check the Mishnah Berurah commentary on that section.
meanings: widely used commentary on Orach Chaim
entries.context_note: A standard practical halachic work frequently cited in Ashkenazi Orthodox settings.

entries.yeshivish_example: What does the Rambam hold here?
entries.plain_english_example: What position does Maimonides take here?
meanings: Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon or his works
entries.context_note: In learning, “the Rambam” often means Maimonides or a passage in Mishneh Torah.

entries.yeshivish_example: Look at the Rashi inside.
entries.plain_english_example: Look at Rashi's commentary in the text.
meanings: Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki or his commentary
entries.context_note: Commonly refers to Rashi’s commentary on Torah or Talmud.

entries.yeshivish_example: The Tosafos asks a kashya.
entries.plain_english_example: The Tosafist commentary raises a difficulty.
entries.context_note: A core layer of traditional Gemara study.

entries.yeshivish_example: The sofer said the mezuzah is pasul.
entries.plain_english_example: The scribe said the mezuzah is invalid under Jewish law.
entries.context_note: Frequently applied to a Sefer Torah, tefillin, mezuzah, sukkah, esrog, or other mitzvah object.

entries.yeshivish_example: Put those old pages in genizah.
entries.plain_english_example: Place those old sacred pages in the repository for respectful disposal.
meanings: respectful storage or burial process for holy writings
entries.context_note: Sacred texts and certain holy objects that may not be discarded normally are placed in genizah.

entries.yeshivish_example: Is this paper shaimos?
entries.plain_english_example: Does this paper require respectful sacred-text disposal?
meanings: items containing divine names or other sanctified text
entries.context_note: In common Ashkenazi speech, shaimos often means papers or books that belong in genizah.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the tashmishei kedushah?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the objects that directly serve items of sanctity?
meanings: objects that directly serve items of sanctity
accessories of sacred objects with special halachic status
entries.context_note: A technical category including objects that directly serve highly sacred items; exact disposal rules depend on the object.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the tashmishei mitzvah?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the objects used to perform a mitzvah?
meanings: objects used to perform a mitzvah
entries.context_note: A halachic category distinct from tashmishei kedushah; treatment after use depends on the object and custom.

entries.yeshivish_example: He paid extra for hidur mitzvah.
entries.plain_english_example: He paid extra to perform the mitzvah with a finer object.
meanings: performing a mitzvah in an especially fine manner
entries.context_note: Used for choosing a more beautiful or higher-quality mitzvah object or performance.

entries.yeshivish_example: Take the tefillin to a sofer.
entries.plain_english_example: Take the tefillin to a qualified sacred scribe.
meanings: scribe trained to write sacred Jewish scrolls
entries.context_note: A sofer writes or repairs items such as Sifrei Torah, tefillin, and mezuzos.

entries.yeshivish_example: The sofer STaM checked the parshiyos.
entries.plain_english_example: The sacred scribe checked the parchment passages.
meanings: scribe specializing in Sefer Torah, tefillin, and mezuzah
entries.context_note: STaM is an acronym for Sefer Torah, Tefillin, Mezuzah.

entries.yeshivish_example: He learned STaM for several years.
entries.plain_english_example: He studied the laws and craft of writing sacred scrolls for several years.
meanings: Sefer Torah, tefillin, and mezuzah scribal field
entries.context_note: An acronym formed from Sefer Torah, Tefillin, and Mezuzah. It refers to the scribal field and its sacred written objects.

entries.yeshivish_example: The letters are written directly on the klaf.
entries.plain_english_example: The letters are written directly on the parchment.
entries.context_note: Used for Sifrei Torah, tefillin parshiyos, and mezuzos.

entries.yeshivish_example: The sofer trimmed his kulmus.
entries.plain_english_example: The scribe trimmed his writing quill.
meanings: writing implement used by a sofer
entries.context_note: Traditionally a reed or feather-type writing instrument prepared for sacred writing.

entries.yeshivish_example: The diyo cracked on one letter.
entries.plain_english_example: The ink cracked on one letter.
entries.context_note: Sacred scrolls require suitable black ink written according to the relevant halachic rules.

entries.yeshivish_example: STaM is written in ksav Ashuris.
entries.plain_english_example: Sacred scrolls are written in the traditional square Hebrew script.
meanings: traditional square Hebrew script used for sacred scrolls
entries.context_note: The formal script used for Sifrei Torah, tefillin, and mezuzos.

entries.yeshivish_example: Two otiyos are touching.
entries.plain_english_example: Two letters are touching.
meanings: Hebrew characters in a sacred text
entries.context_note: In sofrus, the precise form and separation of letters can determine validity.

entries.yeshivish_example: The sofer repaired the tagim.
entries.plain_english_example: The scribe repaired the letter crowns.
meanings: decorative crowns on specified Hebrew letters
entries.context_note: Small crown-like strokes added to designated letters in sacred writing.

entries.yeshivish_example: The klaf already has sirtut.
entries.plain_english_example: The parchment already has ruled guide lines.
entries.context_note: Certain sacred texts require ruled lines before writing.

entries.yeshivish_example: The tear is near the edge of the yeriah.
entries.plain_english_example: The tear is near the edge of the Torah-scroll parchment sheet.
meanings: parchment sheet or panel of a Torah scroll
entries.context_note: A Sefer Torah is assembled from multiple parchment sheets sewn together.

entries.yeshivish_example: The batim are fine but the parshiyos need checking.
entries.plain_english_example: The tefillin boxes are fine but the parchment passages need checking.
meanings: parchment sections, especially in tefillin or mezuzah
entries.context_note: In sofrus and tefillin discussions, parshiyos often means the handwritten parchment passages.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the mukaf gvil?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the letter surrounded by blank parchment?
meanings: requirement that a letter not improperly touch another letter
entries.context_note: A technical scribal rule concerning the blank parchment around letters.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the chok tochos?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the forming a letter by carving away around it rather than writing it?
meanings: forming a letter by carving away around it rather than writing it
prohibited method of creating sacred-script letters
entries.context_note: A technical law in STaM; application can be intricate.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the kesidran?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the written in proper sequence?
entries.context_note: Especially important in tefillin and mezuzah, where certain corrections cannot be made out of sequence.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the shelo kesidran?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the out of the required writing sequence?
meanings: out of the required writing sequence
entries.context_note: A technical STaM issue that can make some later corrections invalid, especially in tefillin and mezuzah.

entries.yeshivish_example: The sefer Torah is out for hagahah.
entries.plain_english_example: The Torah scroll is being professionally checked for errors.
meanings: proofreading or inspection of sacred writing
entries.context_note: Often means checking a Sefer Torah, tefillin, or mezuzah for errors.

entries.yeshivish_example: The magiah found a problem in one word.
entries.plain_english_example: The sacred-text examiner found a problem in one word.
meanings: proofreader or checker of sacred texts
entries.context_note: A person who checks sacred writing for textual or letter-form errors.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the lishmah?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the for the sake of the mitzvah or sanctity?
meanings: for the sake of the mitzvah or sanctity
entries.context_note: A general halachic concept; in STaM it can refer to writing or preparing components with required intent.

entries.yeshivish_example: They took out a sefer Torah for leining.
entries.plain_english_example: They removed a handwritten Torah scroll for the public reading.
meanings: scroll containing the Five Books of Moses
entries.context_note: Written by a qualified sofer on parchment and used for public Torah reading.

entries.yeshivish_example: There are three sifrei Torah in the aron kodesh.
entries.plain_english_example: There are three Torah scrolls in the holy ark.
entries.context_note: Plural used when a synagogue owns or takes out multiple Torah scrolls.

entries.yeshivish_example: The beis knesses is across the street.
entries.plain_english_example: The synagogue is across the street.
meanings: house of assembly for Jewish prayer
entries.context_note: A Hebrew term for synagogue; Yeshivish speech also commonly uses shul.

entries.yeshivish_example: Please open the aron kodesh.
entries.plain_english_example: Please open the holy ark that contains the Torah scrolls.
meanings: holy ark that holds Torah scrolls
entries.context_note: The cabinet at the front of a synagogue where Sifrei Torah are kept.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the heichal?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the sanctuary or Torah ark, especially in Sephardic usage?
meanings: sanctuary or Torah ark, especially in Sephardic usage
entries.context_note: In many Sephardic communities the Torah ark is called the heichal.

entries.yeshivish_example: They changed the paroches before Yom Tov.
entries.plain_english_example: They changed the curtain covering the Torah ark before the festival.
entries.context_note: The decorative curtain associated with the aron kodesh.

entries.yeshivish_example: Put the sefer Torah on the bimah.
entries.plain_english_example: Place the Torah scroll on the reading platform.
meanings: platform or table from which the Torah is read
entries.context_note: Usually the central Torah-reading platform in an Ashkenazi synagogue.

entries.yeshivish_example: The baal koreh used a Torah yad.
entries.plain_english_example: The Torah reader used a pointer to follow the text.
meanings: pointer used to follow text in a Torah scroll
entries.context_note: A hand-shaped pointer used so the reader does not touch the parchment directly.

entries.yeshivish_example: Hold the eitz chaim when you lift the Torah.
entries.plain_english_example: Hold the Torah-scroll handle when you lift it.
meanings: wooden roller or handle of a Torah scroll
entries.context_note: Literally “tree of life”; one of the wooden shafts attached to a Torah scroll.

entries.yeshivish_example: The atzei chaim need repair.
entries.plain_english_example: The Torah-scroll wooden handles need repair.
meanings: wooden rollers or handles of a Torah scroll
entries.context_note: Plural of eitz chaim.

entries.yeshivish_example: The new me'il was donated for the sefer Torah.
entries.plain_english_example: The new cloth Torah mantle was donated for the scroll.
meanings: cloth mantle covering a Torah scroll
entries.context_note: Common Ashkenazi covering placed over a rolled Sefer Torah.

entries.yeshivish_example: Put the gartel around the sefer Torah before the me'il.
entries.plain_english_example: Fasten the Torah binder around the scroll before putting on its mantle.
meanings: belt used around a Torah scroll or as a prayer garment
entries.context_note: The word can mean a Torah binder or a prayer belt depending on context.

entries.yeshivish_example: They polished the rimonim for Yom Tov.
entries.plain_english_example: They polished the Torah-scroll finials for the festival.
meanings: decorative finials placed on Torah-scroll handles
entries.context_note: Often silver ornaments placed over the upper ends of the atzei chaim.

entries.yeshivish_example: The keser Torah is kept in the cabinet.
entries.plain_english_example: The Torah crown is kept in the cabinet.
meanings: decorative crown placed on a Torah scroll
entries.context_note: An ornamental crown used on some Torah scrolls.

entries.yeshivish_example: The tas has the donor's inscription.
entries.plain_english_example: The Torah breastplate has the donor's inscription.
meanings: decorative metal plate hung on a Torah scroll
entries.context_note: An Ashkenazi Torah ornament, often suspended from the upper handles.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the tik?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the rigid case for a Torah scroll?
meanings: rigid case for a Torah scroll
entries.context_note: Many Sephardic and Mizrahi Torah scrolls are housed in a rigid tik rather than a cloth mantle.

entries.yeshivish_example: He got pesicha for Neilah.
entries.plain_english_example: He received the honor of opening the Torah ark for the closing service.
meanings: honor of opening the Torah ark
entries.context_note: In Ashkenazi synagogue usage, pesicha often means being honored with opening the aron kodesh.

entries.yeshivish_example: We are up to hotzaas Sefer Torah.
entries.plain_english_example: The service has reached the removal of the Torah scroll from the ark.
meanings: taking the Torah scroll out of the ark
removal of the Torah for public reading
entries.context_note: Refers to the part of the service when the Torah is removed from the ark.

entries.yeshivish_example: The hachnasas Sefer Torah is Sunday.
entries.plain_english_example: The Torah-scroll dedication procession is Sunday.
meanings: bringing a Torah scroll into a synagogue
entries.context_note: Often means the celebratory dedication and procession of a newly completed Sefer Torah.

entries.yeshivish_example: Who is leining this Shabbos?
entries.plain_english_example: Who is reading the Torah publicly this Sabbath?
meanings: public chanting or reading of the Torah
entries.context_note: A Yiddish-derived term widely used in Ashkenazi Orthodox English.

entries.yeshivish_example: The baal koreh knows the whole parsha.
entries.plain_english_example: The Torah reader knows the entire weekly portion.
meanings: person who chants the public Torah reading
entries.context_note: The person who reads the Torah aloud for the congregation.

entries.yeshivish_example: Ask the baal kriah about the trop.
entries.plain_english_example: Ask the Torah reader about the cantillation.
meanings: person responsible for the public reading
entries.context_note: Another common term for the baal koreh.

entries.yeshivish_example: The kriah was very clear.
entries.plain_english_example: The public Torah reading was very clear.
meanings: public Torah reading, depending on context
entries.context_note: Context determines whether it means reading generally or a formal liturgical reading. This transliteration can collide with the mourning term keriah/kriah (קריעה), meaning ritual tearing; the Aleph-Beis spelling and context distinguish them.

entries.yeshivish_example: Krias haTorah starts after Shacharis.
entries.plain_english_example: The public Torah reading begins after the morning prayer service.
meanings: reading of the Torah in synagogue
entries.context_note: Formal Hebrew term for the communal Torah-reading service.

entries.yeshivish_example: What is the parsha this week?
entries.plain_english_example: What is the weekly Torah portion this week?
entries.context_note: In weekly conversation, usually means the weekly Torah reading.

entries.yeshivish_example: The vort is on the parshas hashavua.
entries.plain_english_example: The Torah thought is about the weekly portion.
meanings: Torah reading assigned to the week
entries.context_note: Literally the portion of the week.

entries.yeshivish_example: Which sedra are we reading?
entries.plain_english_example: Which weekly Torah portion are we reading?
entries.context_note: An older/common Ashkenazi term for the weekly parsha.

entries.yeshivish_example: He is doing the haftorah for his bar mitzvah.
entries.plain_english_example: He is chanting the prophetic reading for his bar mitzvah.
meanings: prophetic reading following the Torah reading
entries.context_note: A selection from the Prophets read after the Torah portion on designated days.

entries.yeshivish_example: Who has maftir this week?
entries.plain_english_example: Who has the final Torah aliyah and haftarah assignment this week?
meanings: final Torah aliyah associated with the haftarah reader
entries.context_note: The maftir aliyah precedes the haftarah; on special days it may be read from an additional scroll.

entries.yeshivish_example: The oleh should stand next to the baal koreh.
entries.plain_english_example: The person called to the Torah should stand next to the reader.
meanings: person called to the Torah for an aliyah
entries.context_note: Literally one who goes up; in synagogue context the person receiving an aliyah.

entries.yeshivish_example: He got hagbah today.
entries.plain_english_example: He received the honor of lifting and displaying the Torah scroll today.
meanings: lifting the Torah scroll for display
entries.context_note: The ritual lifting and displaying of the Torah scroll around the conclusion of the reading.

entries.yeshivish_example: His son did gelilah.
entries.plain_english_example: His son received the honor of dressing the Torah scroll.
meanings: rolling and dressing the Torah scroll
entries.context_note: The honor of closing, binding, and dressing the Torah after hagbah.

entries.yeshivish_example: He is practicing the trop.
entries.plain_english_example: He is practicing the Torah-reading cantillation.
meanings: cantillation melody or marks used for Torah and haftarah reading
entries.context_note: Yeshivish/Ashkenazi term for the cantillation system; Hebrew terminology is taamei hamikra.

entries.yeshivish_example: The taamei hamikra change the phrasing.
entries.plain_english_example: The biblical cantillation marks affect the phrasing.
entries.context_note: Formal Hebrew term for the accent and cantillation marks used when chanting Tanach.

entries.yeshivish_example: Read the next pasuk again.
entries.plain_english_example: Read the next biblical verse again.
entries.context_note: Very common in learning and Torah-reading conversation.

entries.yeshivish_example: These pesukim are in the haftorah.
entries.plain_english_example: These biblical verses are in the prophetic reading.
entries.context_note: Plural of pasuk.

entries.yeshivish_example: Did you bring your tefillin?
entries.plain_english_example: Did you bring the ritual leather boxes worn for weekday prayer?
meanings: pair of black leather boxes containing Torah passages worn for weekday prayer
entries.context_note: The mitzvah uses one tefillin on the arm and one on the head.

entries.yeshivish_example: Hanachas tefillin is before Shacharis.
entries.plain_english_example: Putting on tefillin is before the morning service.
entries.context_note: The act or mitzvah performance of placing and fastening tefillin.

entries.yeshivish_example: The tefillin shel yad goes on the arm.
entries.plain_english_example: The arm tefillin is placed on the upper arm.
meanings: tefillin worn on the upper arm
entries.context_note: Contains the four Torah passages written together on one parchment scroll.

entries.yeshivish_example: Check that the tefillin shel rosh is centered.
entries.plain_english_example: Check that the head tefillin is centered.
entries.context_note: Contains the four passages in separate compartments.

entries.yeshivish_example: The batim need to stay square.
entries.plain_english_example: The tefillin boxes need to retain their required square form.
entries.context_note: Literally houses; in tefillin context, the black leather box structures.

entries.yeshivish_example: The retzuos are starting to fade.
entries.plain_english_example: The tefillin straps are starting to lose their black color.
entries.context_note: Black leather straps used to fasten the shel yad and shel rosh.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the ketzitzah?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the main cube of a tefillin box?
meanings: main cube of a tefillin box
upper box containing the parchment passages
entries.context_note: A technical term for the square upper section of the tefillin bayis.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the titura?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the base or platform of a tefillin box?
meanings: base or platform of a tefillin box
lower base of the tefillin housing
entries.context_note: A technical tefillin-construction term for the base beneath the main cube.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the maabarta?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the passage or bridge through which the tefillin strap runs?
meanings: passage or bridge through which the tefillin strap runs
strap channel of the tefillin housing
entries.context_note: A technical structural component of tefillin.

entries.yeshivish_example: The kesher shel yad became loose.
entries.plain_english_example: The knot of the arm tefillin became loose.
entries.context_note: The specially formed knot associated with the arm tefillin.

entries.yeshivish_example: The kesher shel rosh needs adjustment.
entries.plain_english_example: The knot of the head tefillin needs adjustment.
entries.context_note: The specially formed knot at the back of the head-tefillin straps.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the shin shel tefillin?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the raised Hebrew shin formed on the head-tefillin box?
meanings: raised Hebrew shin formed on the head-tefillin box
entries.context_note: The shel rosh has molded shin forms on its sides.

entries.yeshivish_example: These are my Rashi tefillin.
entries.plain_english_example: These are my tefillin arranged according to Rashi's ordering.
meanings: tefillin arranged according to Rashi’s ordering
entries.context_note: Refers to the order of the parchment passages according to Rashi.

entries.yeshivish_example: He also puts on Rabbeinu Tam tefillin.
entries.plain_english_example: He also wears an additional pair arranged according to Rabbeinu Tam.
meanings: tefillin arranged according to Rabbeinu Tam’s ordering
entries.context_note: Some people wear an additional pair with the passage order associated with Rabbeinu Tam.

entries.yeshivish_example: The batim macher repaired the corner.
entries.plain_english_example: The tefillin-box craftsman repaired the corner.
entries.context_note: A Yiddish/Hebrew occupational term used in the tefillin trade.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the giddin?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the sinew thread used in sacred-object construction?
meanings: sinew thread used in sacred-object construction
animal sinews used for sewing tefillin or Torah sheets
entries.context_note: Used in specific construction and sewing requirements for STaM items.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the ribua?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the squareness?
meanings: required square form of tefillin components
entries.context_note: Tefillin have detailed squareness requirements; practical measurements belong to sofrus expertise.

entries.yeshivish_example: My tefillin bag is in the locker.
entries.plain_english_example: My tefillin pouch is in the locker.
meanings: protective bag or case for tefillin
entries.context_note: Common everyday term for the bag in which tefillin are stored and carried.

entries.yeshivish_example: His tzitzis are showing under his shirt.
entries.plain_english_example: The ritual fringes of his four-cornered garment are showing under his shirt.
meanings: ritual fringes attached to a four-cornered garment
entries.context_note: In Yeshivish, tzitzis can refer either to the fringes or to the tallis katan garment itself.

entries.yeshivish_example: He put on his tallis before davening.
entries.plain_english_example: He put on his prayer shawl before praying.
entries.context_note: In Ashkenazi pronunciation commonly tallis; context may mean a tallis gadol specifically.

entries.yeshivish_example: He needs a new tallis katan.
entries.plain_english_example: He needs a new small four-cornered tzitzis garment.
meanings: small four-cornered garment worn with tzitzis
entries.context_note: Usually worn under or over clothing throughout the day.

entries.yeshivish_example: The tallis gadol is in his bag.
entries.plain_english_example: The large prayer shawl is in his bag.
meanings: large prayer shawl worn during prayer
entries.context_note: The larger tallis worn over the shoulders for prayer according to community custom.

entries.yeshivish_example: The child started wearing arba kanfos.
entries.plain_english_example: The child started wearing a four-cornered tzitzis garment.
entries.context_note: Literally four corners; often another name for the small tzitzis garment.

entries.yeshivish_example: One of the chutim tore.
entries.plain_english_example: One of the tzitzis strings tore.
entries.context_note: In tzitzis discussion, usually the strings tied through the corners.

entries.yeshivish_example: The gedilim were tied lishmah.
entries.plain_english_example: The ritual fringes were tied with the required mitzvah intention.
entries.context_note: A Torah term associated with the fringes attached to a four-cornered garment.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the techeles?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the blue-dyed thread used in tzitzis according to traditions that identify it?
meanings: blue-dyed thread used in tzitzis according to traditions that identify it
entries.context_note: Modern use and identification of techeles varies among communities and authorities.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the pesil techeles?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the thread of techeles?
entries.context_note: Biblical phrase for the blue thread among the tzitzis.

entries.yeshivish_example: The tallis has a silver atarah.
entries.plain_english_example: The prayer shawl has a silver decorative neckband.
meanings: decorative neckband or crown on a tallis
entries.context_note: Some talleisim have a decorative atarah along the edge worn at the head or neck.

entries.yeshivish_example: His tallis bag has his Hebrew name on it.
entries.plain_english_example: His prayer-shawl bag has his Hebrew name on it.
entries.context_note: Often paired with a matching tefillin bag.

entries.yeshivish_example: Is this beged obligated in tzitzis?
entries.plain_english_example: Does this garment require ritual fringes?
entries.context_note: In tzitzis halacha, refers to the garment to which the fringes are attached.

entries.yeshivish_example: The hole is too close to the edge of the kanaf.
entries.plain_english_example: The hole is too close to the edge of the garment corner.
entries.context_note: In tzitzis discussion, a corner of the garment where the strings are attached.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the chulya?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the group or segment of tzitzis windings?
meanings: group or segment of tzitzis windings
entries.context_note: A technical term for a grouping of wraps in certain tzitzis-tying systems.

entries.yeshivish_example: Count the krichos again.
entries.plain_english_example: Count the tzitzis windings again.
meanings: windings or wraps of tzitzis strings
entries.context_note: Refers to the wraps made while tying tzitzis.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the l'shem mitzvas tzitzis?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the for the sake of the mitzvah of tzitzis?
meanings: for the sake of the mitzvah of tzitzis
intentional preparation for the tzitzis mitzvah
entries.context_note: Phrase describing the required or preferred intent during certain stages of tzitzis preparation or tying.

entries.yeshivish_example: The new office needs a mezuzah.
entries.plain_english_example: The new office doorway needs a mezuzah scroll.
meanings: parchment scroll affixed to a Jewish doorway
entries.context_note: The essential mitzvah object is the handwritten parchment scroll; the outer case protects it.

entries.yeshivish_example: We are checking all the mezuzos in the house.
entries.plain_english_example: We are checking all the mezuzah scrolls in the house.
entries.context_note: Common plural in Ashkenazi/Yeshivish speech.

entries.yeshivish_example: The mezuzah case cracked but the klaf is fine.
entries.plain_english_example: The protective mezuzah case cracked but the parchment is fine.
meanings: protective case holding a mezuzah scroll
entries.context_note: The case is not itself the written mezuzah scroll and should not be confused with it.

entries.yeshivish_example: Make sure there is a real mezuzah scroll inside.
entries.plain_english_example: Make sure there is a handwritten kosher parchment inside the case.
meanings: handwritten parchment inside a mezuzah case
entries.context_note: Contains prescribed Torah passages handwritten by a qualified sofer.

entries.yeshivish_example: The kevias mezuzah is after Mincha.
entries.plain_english_example: The mezuzah installation is after the afternoon service.
entries.context_note: The act or ceremony of properly fixing the mezuzah to the doorway.

entries.yeshivish_example: Who is going to be kovea mezuzah?
entries.plain_english_example: Who is going to affix the mezuzah?
entries.context_note: Used as a verb or in discussion of the blessing for affixing a mezuzah.

entries.yeshivish_example: It is time for bedikas mezuzos.
entries.plain_english_example: It is time to have the mezuzah scrolls inspected.
entries.context_note: A sofer or qualified checker examines the lettering and parchment for problems.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the heker tzir?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the door-hinge indicator used in some mezuzah-placement questions?
meanings: door-hinge indicator used in some mezuzah-placement questions
entries.context_note: A technical factor used in some halachic discussions of which side of a doorway receives the mezuzah; application varies.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do you have the makom mezuzah?
entries.plain_english_example: Do you have the proper location for placing a mezuzah on a doorway?
meanings: proper location for placing a mezuzah on a doorway
entries.context_note: Placement has detailed halachic requirements regarding side and height.

entries.yeshivish_example: He keeps an extra kippah in the car.
entries.plain_english_example: He keeps an extra Jewish head covering in the car.
entries.context_note: Common Hebrew term for a Jewish head covering.

entries.yeshivish_example: The boy lost his yarmulke.
entries.plain_english_example: The boy lost his Jewish skullcap.
entries.context_note: Yiddish/Ashkenazi term corresponding to kippah.

entries.yeshivish_example: She bought a new sheitel for the wedding.
entries.plain_english_example: She bought a new hair-covering wig for the wedding.
meanings: wig worn as a married woman’s hair covering
entries.context_note: Common in many Orthodox communities; practices and norms vary.

entries.yeshivish_example: She wore a tichel today.
entries.plain_english_example: She wore a headscarf as her hair covering today.
meanings: headscarf used as a hair covering
entries.context_note: A Yiddish term for a scarf used by many married Orthodox women as a hair covering.

entries.yeshivish_example: Her mitpachas matched the dress.
entries.plain_english_example: Her headscarf matched the dress.
meanings: scarf, often a married woman’s hair covering
entries.context_note: Modern Hebrew term often used alongside Yiddish tichel.

entries.yeshivish_example: He brought his kittel for Yom Kippur.
entries.plain_english_example: He brought his white ritual robe for the Day of Atonement.
meanings: white garment worn on certain Jewish occasions
entries.context_note: Worn according to community custom on occasions such as Yom Kippur, the Pesach Seder, or by a chosson.

entries.yeshivish_example: The new suit was checked for shatnez.
entries.plain_english_example: The new suit was checked for a forbidden wool-linen mixture.
meanings: prohibition against wearing specified mixtures of wool and linen
entries.context_note: Commonly discussed when checking suits and garments.

entries.yeshivish_example: Take the jacket to a shatnez checker.
entries.plain_english_example: Take the jacket to a specialist who checks for forbidden wool-linen mixtures.
meanings: person or service that checks garments for shatnez
entries.context_note: A specialist or laboratory that examines clothing for prohibited wool-linen mixtures.

entries.yeshivish_example: Put a dollar in the pushka.
entries.plain_english_example: Put a dollar in the charity box.
entries.context_note: A common Yiddish term for a small charity box kept at home, school, or synagogue.

entries.yeshivish_example: There is a tzedakah box by the door.
entries.plain_english_example: There is a charity collection box by the door.
meanings: box used to collect charitable donations
entries.context_note: English/Yeshivish phrase corresponding to Hebrew kupat tzedakah and Yiddish pushka.

entries.yeshivish_example: The leichter were her grandmother's.
entries.plain_english_example: The Sabbath candlesticks belonged to her grandmother.
entries.context_note: In Yiddish family usage, lighter or leichter often refers to the Shabbos candlesticks.

entries.yeshivish_example: The kiddush cup is on the table.
entries.plain_english_example: The cup used for Kiddush is on the table.
meanings: ritual wine cup for sanctifying Shabbos or Yom Tov
entries.context_note: Often a dedicated silver or decorative cup, though the mitzvah does not require a specific material.

entries.yeshivish_example: They filled the kos shel bracha.
entries.plain_english_example: They filled the ritual cup used for the blessing.
meanings: cup of wine used for a blessing or ritual
entries.context_note: A broader term than kiddush cup; can apply to several ceremonies involving a cup of wine.

entries.yeshivish_example: Put the challah cover over the loaves.
entries.plain_english_example: Place the ritual cloth over the challah loaves.
meanings: cloth used to cover challah at a Shabbos or Yom Tov meal
entries.context_note: A common ritual table object used while making Kiddush and Hamotzi.

entries.yeshivish_example: We need a new Havdalah candle.
entries.plain_english_example: We need a new multi-wick candle for the Havdalah ceremony.
entries.context_note: The candle used for the blessing over fire during Havdalah.

entries.yeshivish_example: Pass the besamim around.
entries.plain_english_example: Pass the fragrant spices around.
meanings: spices used for the Havdalah blessing
entries.context_note: At Havdalah, fragrant spices are smelled with a blessing in the standard Saturday-night service.

entries.yeshivish_example: The besamim box is next to the candle.
entries.plain_english_example: The spice container is next to the Havdalah candle.
entries.context_note: Often decorative; the mitzvah concerns smelling the fragrance rather than a particular container.

entries.yeshivish_example: He set up negel vasser by the bed.
entries.plain_english_example: He prepared water by the bed for ritual hand washing upon waking.
meanings: ritual washing setup used upon waking
entries.context_note: Yiddish term for the water and practice of washing hands upon waking; customs vary in details.

entries.yeshivish_example: The natla is by the sink.
entries.plain_english_example: The ritual hand-washing cup is by the sink.
meanings: handled cup used for ritual hand washing
entries.context_note: Common term for the cup used for netilas yadayim.

entries.yeshivish_example: There are bentchers on every table.
entries.plain_english_example: There are Grace-after-Meals booklets on every table.
meanings: booklet containing Grace after Meals and often songs or blessings
entries.context_note: Commonly used at Shabbos meals, weddings, and other celebrations.

entries.yeshivish_example: We sang zemiros after the first course.
entries.plain_english_example: We sang Sabbath table songs after the first course.
meanings: religious songs, especially for Shabbos meals
entries.context_note: Often printed in a bentcher or sung from memory at Shabbos meals.

entries.yeshivish_example: His Gemara is on the shtender.
entries.plain_english_example: His Talmud volume is on the study lectern.
meanings: lectern or bookstand used for prayer or Torah study
entries.context_note: A common piece of synagogue and beis-midраш furniture.

entries.yeshivish_example: The mechitzah was moved for the larger event.
entries.plain_english_example: The synagogue partition was moved for the larger event.
meanings: partition separating sections in an Orthodox synagogue
entries.context_note: Usually refers to the partition between men’s and women’s prayer areas; forms vary by community and synagogue.

entries.yeshivish_example: There are more seats upstairs in the ezras nashim.
entries.plain_english_example: There are more seats upstairs in the women's section of the synagogue.
entries.context_note: Literally women’s section; may be on the same floor, a balcony, or another designated area.

entries.yeshivish_example: The ner tamid is above the aron kodesh.
entries.plain_english_example: The synagogue's eternal light is above the holy ark.
entries.context_note: A light customarily kept near or above the aron kodesh.

entries.yeshivish_example: He davens in the shtibl around the corner.
entries.plain_english_example: He prays in the small synagogue around the corner.
entries.context_note: A Yiddish term especially common for a small or neighborhood prayer house.

entries.yeshivish_example: Putting on tefillin is a mitzvas aseh.
entries.plain_english_example: Putting on tefillin is a positive commandment.
entries.context_note: Contrasts with a negative commandment, mitzvas lo saaseh.

entries.yeshivish_example: Shatnez involves a mitzvas lo sa'aseh.
entries.plain_english_example: The prohibition of shatnez is a negative commandment.
meanings: Torah prohibition stated as something not to do
entries.context_note: Often shortened conversationally to a lo saaseh.

entries.yeshivish_example: Is there a chiyuv to do it now?
entries.plain_english_example: Is there a halachic obligation to do it now?
entries.context_note: Can describe a person’s obligation or the level of requirement of an act.

entries.yeshivish_example: In that case he may be patur.
entries.plain_english_example: In that case he may be exempt from the obligation.
meanings: not obligated in a particular requirement
entries.context_note: Does not necessarily mean an act is forbidden; it means the obligation does not apply in the stated way.

entries.yeshivish_example: They learned the halachos of taharas hamishpacha before the wedding.
entries.plain_english_example: They learned the Jewish family-purity laws before the wedding.
meanings: the laws governing niddah, separation, and mikvah
entries.context_note: Ashkenazi/Yeshivish pronunciation of taharat hamishpacha. It is an umbrella term for the laws of niddah and mikvah.

entries.yeshivish_example: She has the halachic status of niddah.
entries.plain_english_example: She is in the halachic status in which the couple observes the niddah restrictions.
meanings: the halachic status associated with specified uterine bleeding
a woman in that halachic status
entries.context_note: In practical Orthodox usage, the status continues until the required taharah process and valid mikvah immersion are completed.

entries.yeshivish_example: After a valid tevilah she is tehorah.
entries.plain_english_example: After a valid immersion she is no longer in the niddah status.
entries.context_note: Feminine form of tahor; in taharas hamishpacha it commonly describes the status after completing the required process and immersion.

entries.yeshivish_example: The term tahor means ritually pure.
entries.plain_english_example: The term means ritually pure.
entries.context_note: General ritual-purity term. The feminine form tehorah is more common in family-purity discussions.

entries.yeshivish_example: The older terminology may describe the status as temeiah.
entries.plain_english_example: The older terminology may describe the status as ritually impure.
entries.context_note: Feminine form of tamei. In modern family-purity discussion, niddah is often the more precise practical term.

entries.yeshivish_example: Tamei is the masculine form of the ritual-impurity term.
entries.plain_english_example: Tamei means ritually impure in halachic terminology.
entries.context_note: A broad ritual-purity term with applications beyond taharas hamishpacha.

entries.yeshivish_example: She is beginning the taharah process.
entries.plain_english_example: She is beginning the process of returning to a permitted family-purity status.
entries.context_note: In this context it often refers to the process that includes a hefsek taharah, seven clean days, and mikvah immersion.

entries.yeshivish_example: The sugya uses the language of tumah and taharah.
entries.plain_english_example: The Talmudic discussion uses the language of ritual impurity and purity.
meanings: the state of being tamei or temeiah
entries.context_note: A broad halachic concept that extends far beyond niddah.

entries.yeshivish_example: She plans to make a hefsek taharah before sunset.
entries.plain_english_example: She plans to perform the examination that establishes that uterine bleeding has ceased before sunset.
meanings: examination used to establish that bleeding has ceased
the step that begins the transition toward the seven clean days
entries.context_note: A core step in the taharah process. Practical timing and procedure should follow the applicable halachic guidance.

entries.yeshivish_example: She is in the middle of the shivah neki'im.
entries.plain_english_example: She is in the middle of the seven clean days.
meanings: seven blood-free clean days counted before mikvah immersion
entries.context_note: The count begins after a valid hefsek taharah according to the applicable halachic rules.

entries.yeshivish_example: She had a shayla about a bedikah.
entries.plain_english_example: She had a halachic question about an internal examination.
meanings: halachic internal examination performed with a cloth
entries.context_note: In this context, bedikah refers to an internal examination used during the taharah process or at specified anticipated-cycle times.

entries.yeshivish_example: She used a clean eid bedikah.
entries.plain_english_example: She used a clean white cloth designated for the halachic examination.
meanings: cloth used for a bedikah examination
entries.context_note: Eid or ed literally means witness. As a standalone transliteration it is ambiguous outside this context.

entries.yeshivish_example: She asked whether the moch dachuk was required in her case.
entries.plain_english_example: She asked whether the cloth kept in place around sunset after the hefsek was required in her case.
meanings: bedikah cloth retained internally around the transition into the seven clean days
entries.context_note: A taharah-process term. Exact timing and when it may be omitted are practical halachic questions.

entries.yeshivish_example: She found a kesem and asked whether it affected her status.
entries.plain_english_example: She found a stain and asked whether it had halachic significance.
meanings: stain considered under the laws of niddah
entries.context_note: Not every stain changes niddah status; factors such as color, size, surface, and circumstances can matter.

entries.yeshivish_example: The rav considered whether it was dam makkah.
entries.plain_english_example: The rabbi considered whether the blood came from a wound or irritation rather than uterine bleeding.
meanings: blood from a wound, injury, or irritation
entries.context_note: Used to distinguish blood from a local injury or irritation from uterine bleeding for niddah analysis.

entries.yeshivish_example: They learned the halachos of dam betulim before the wedding.
entries.plain_english_example: They learned the laws concerning hymenal bleeding before the wedding.
meanings: hymenal bleeding associated with initial marital relations
entries.context_note: A specialized family-purity term with practical rules distinct from ordinary menstrual bleeding.

entries.yeshivish_example: The kallah teacher mentioned the concept of dam chimud.
entries.plain_english_example: The bridal teacher mentioned the halachic concept of bleeding associated with anticipation of marriage.
meanings: bleeding associated in halachic literature with excitement or anticipation of marriage
entries.context_note: A technical pre-wedding niddah concept; practical application should be handled by a qualified halachic authority.

entries.yeshivish_example: The shayla may depend on whether there was a hargashah.
entries.plain_english_example: The question may depend on whether there was a halachically relevant bodily sensation.
meanings: halachically relevant sensation associated with uterine bleeding
entries.context_note: A technical criterion in niddah law. What qualifies as a hargashah is a matter of halachic analysis.

entries.yeshivish_example: They discussed whether the kesem was larger than a gris.
entries.plain_english_example: They discussed whether the stain exceeded the relevant halachic size measure.
meanings: halachic area measurement used in the laws of stains
entries.context_note: The practical measurement used for a gris is technical and should not be inferred from this glossary entry alone.

entries.yeshivish_example: The surface may be mekabel tumah.
entries.plain_english_example: The surface may be susceptible to ritual impurity.
entries.context_note: In the laws of ketamim, the status of the surface on which a stain is found can be relevant.

entries.yeshivish_example: That disposable surface may be eino mekabel tumah.
entries.plain_english_example: That disposable surface may not be susceptible to ritual impurity.
entries.context_note: Used in stain analysis; the classification of particular materials can require halachic judgment.

entries.yeshivish_example: She is going to the mikvah tonight.
entries.plain_english_example: She is going to the ritual immersion pool tonight.
meanings: facility containing a halachically valid body of water for immersion
entries.context_note: In everyday Orthodox usage, the word often refers both to the ritual pool and to the facility housing it.

entries.yeshivish_example: Her tevilah is scheduled for tonight.
entries.plain_english_example: Her ritual immersion is scheduled for tonight.
entries.context_note: The noun for immersion. In family-purity discussion it usually refers to immersion that concludes the niddah period.

entries.yeshivish_example: She plans to toivel after nightfall.
entries.plain_english_example: She plans to immerse in the mikvah after nightfall.
entries.context_note: Yeshivish often uses a Hebrew-derived verb as an English verb. Hebrew gendered forms differ in fully Hebrew speech.

entries.yeshivish_example: They discussed the importance of tevilah bizmanah.
entries.plain_english_example: They discussed immersion at its appropriate halachic time.
meanings: mikvah immersion at the appropriate time
entries.context_note: A timing concept in mikvah law; scheduling details can depend on circumstances and calendar constraints.

entries.yeshivish_example: She left enough time for chafifah before the mikvah.
entries.plain_english_example: She left enough time for the washing and cleansing done in preparation for immersion.
meanings: cleansing and washing in preparation for mikvah immersion
entries.context_note: Preparation intended to remove material that could interfere with immersion.

entries.yeshivish_example: She asked whether the bandage was a chatzitzah.
entries.plain_english_example: She asked whether the bandage constituted a barrier to the mikvah water.
meanings: barrier between the body and mikvah water
intervening substance that can affect immersion
entries.context_note: Whether a particular item is a disqualifying chatzitzah can depend on detailed halachic criteria.

entries.yeshivish_example: She did the iyun before tevilah.
entries.plain_english_example: She inspected her body for possible barriers before immersion.
meanings: inspection for possible chatzitzos before mikvah immersion
entries.context_note: In yeshiva settings iyun can also mean in-depth study, so context is essential.

entries.yeshivish_example: The balanit was available to assist at the mikvah.
entries.plain_english_example: The mikvah attendant was available to assist.
entries.context_note: Common Modern Hebrew term for the woman who attends the mikvah and may observe that immersion is complete.

entries.yeshivish_example: The halacha of beit hastarim came up during mikvah preparation.
entries.plain_english_example: The law concerning accessible hidden areas of the body came up during mikvah preparation.
meanings: accessible hidden parts of the body considered in immersion preparation
entries.context_note: A technical mikvah-preparation category. These areas have specific rules concerning cleanliness and water contact.

entries.yeshivish_example: The item may be considered balua rather than an external chatzitzah.
entries.plain_english_example: The item may be considered internally absorbed or located rather than an external barrier.
meanings: something in a normally inaccessible internal area
entries.context_note: Technical terminology used when analyzing whether material in an inaccessible body area affects immersion.

entries.yeshivish_example: The shiur discussed the requirement of mayim chayim in different immersion contexts.
entries.plain_english_example: The lesson discussed naturally sourced living water in different immersion contexts.
meanings: naturally sourced water used in ritual-purity law
entries.context_note: The exact water requirements differ among types of ritual immersion; this is a glossary-level definition.

entries.yeshivish_example: A mikvah requires the halachic volume of arba'im se'ah.
entries.plain_english_example: A mikvah requires the halachically specified minimum volume traditionally described as forty seah.
meanings: traditional minimum-volume measure associated with a mikvah
entries.context_note: The conversion of forty seah into modern units differs among halachic measurements and should not be inferred from this glossary entry.

entries.yeshivish_example: The minimum volume is expressed in se'ah.
entries.plain_english_example: The minimum volume is expressed using the traditional seah measure.
entries.context_note: Modern-unit conversions vary according to halachic measurement systems.

entries.yeshivish_example: The mikvah uses a bor hashakah.
entries.plain_english_example: The mikvah uses a connected reservoir arrangement involving hashakah.
meanings: halachic connection of water bodies used in mikvah construction
entries.context_note: Technical mikvah-construction term; exact engineering and halachic requirements vary by design and authority.

entries.yeshivish_example: The design uses z'riah to connect or validate the water system.
entries.plain_english_example: The design uses a halachic water-introduction method known as zeriah.
entries.context_note: Technical mikvah-construction term whose implementation varies among accepted designs.

entries.yeshivish_example: The mikvah has a bor hashakah beside the immersion pool.
entries.plain_english_example: The mikvah has a reservoir used for halachic water connection beside the immersion pool.
meanings: reservoir used for hashakah in a mikvah system
entries.context_note: Technical construction terminology; not every mikvah uses the same configuration.

entries.yeshivish_example: The plans show a separate bor z'riah.
entries.plain_english_example: The plans show a separate reservoir used for the zeriah method.
meanings: reservoir used for zeriah in a mikvah system
entries.context_note: Technical construction terminology; designs and halachic preferences differ.

entries.yeshivish_example: She keeps track of her veset carefully.
entries.plain_english_example: She keeps track of the halachically relevant pattern or anticipated time of menstruation.
meanings: anticipated time or circumstance for menstruation
entries.context_note: In niddah law, veset can refer to a cycle pattern or to an anticipated period requiring observance.

entries.yeshivish_example: She asked whether she established a veset kavua.
entries.plain_english_example: She asked whether she had established a halachically regular menstrual pattern.
entries.context_note: Establishing and uprooting a veset kavua follows technical halachic rules.

entries.yeshivish_example: This is still a veset she'eino kavua.
entries.plain_english_example: This is still a menstrual pattern that is not halachically established as regular.
meanings: non-established or irregular halachic menstrual pattern
entries.context_note: Contrasts with a veset kavua.

entries.yeshivish_example: She has a recurring veset haguf.
entries.plain_english_example: She has a recurring premenstrual bodily sign that may form a halachic pattern.
meanings: menstrual pattern based on recurring physical symptoms
entries.context_note: A technical veset category based on bodily signs rather than only dates or intervals.

entries.yeshivish_example: Her pattern may be a veset chatzi kavua.
entries.plain_english_example: Her pattern may be a semi-regular halachic menstrual pattern.
meanings: semi-regular menstrual pattern in halachic terminology
entries.context_note: A specialized pattern category; practical consequences depend on the precise history.

entries.yeshivish_example: She recorded a possible veset hachodesh.
entries.plain_english_example: She recorded a possible menstrual pattern based on the Hebrew-calendar date.
meanings: menstrual pattern based on a recurring Hebrew-calendar date
entries.context_note: A form of veset based on the date of the Hebrew month.

entries.yeshivish_example: The calendar shows a veset haflagah.
entries.plain_english_example: The calendar shows a menstrual pattern based on the interval between periods.
meanings: menstrual pattern based on a recurring interval
entries.context_note: A form of veset based on the interval between the beginnings of menstrual flows.

entries.yeshivish_example: The rav checked whether the dates formed a veset hadilug.
