entries.plain_english_example: The rabbi checked whether the dates formed a progressively shifting menstrual pattern.
meanings: progressively shifting menstrual pattern recognized in halachic cycle law
entries.context_note: An advanced veset category; exact establishment rules are technical.

entries.yeshivish_example: That date falls in the daytime onah.
entries.plain_english_example: That date falls in the relevant daytime halachic time period.
meanings: halachic time period of a day or night
marital obligation in the phrase mitzvas onah
entries.context_note: The word has several halachic meanings; context is required.

entries.yeshivish_example: She marked the onah beinonit on her calendar.
entries.plain_english_example: She marked the standard average-cycle anticipation period on her calendar.
meanings: standard average interval used as an anticipated menstruation period
entries.context_note: A technical calendar concept in the laws of vesatot; calculation practices should follow the applicable halachic authority.

entries.yeshivish_example: They observe the onas perishah when the period is anticipated.
entries.plain_english_example: They observe the prescribed separation period when menstruation is halachically anticipated.
meanings: time when specified niddah precautions are observed because menstruation is expected
entries.context_note: Plural forms include onot perishah. Practical requirements depend on the type of veset and ruling followed.

entries.yeshivish_example: She marked the yom hachodesh for the next month.
entries.plain_english_example: She marked the corresponding Hebrew-calendar date for the next month.
meanings: same Hebrew-calendar date in the following month used for cycle anticipation
entries.context_note: One of the standard calendar dates tracked in vesatot practice.

entries.yeshivish_example: Her haflagah was shorter this month.
entries.plain_english_example: The interval between the beginnings of her menstrual periods was shorter this month.
meanings: interval between menstrual periods used in halachic cycle tracking
entries.context_note: The interval is used in calculating a veset haflagah.

entries.yeshivish_example: Their minhag is to observe the Or Zarua onah.
entries.plain_english_example: Their custom is to observe the additional anticipation period associated with the Or Zarua practice.
meanings: practice of observing an additional onah before an anticipated menstruation period
entries.context_note: Named for the halachic source. This is not observed identically in all communities.

entries.yeshivish_example: The question is whether the veset was ne'ekar.
entries.plain_english_example: The question is whether the established menstrual pattern was halachically uprooted.
meanings: uprooted or cancelled, especially an established veset
entries.context_note: Technical term for a veset that no longer requires observance after the conditions for uprooting it have been met.

entries.yeshivish_example: They observe the harchakos while she is niddah.
entries.plain_english_example: They observe the prescribed distancing rules while she is in niddah status.
meanings: restrictions designed to avoid physical contact during niddah
entries.context_note: The specific harchakos include multiple practical rules and can vary in details by accepted halachic practice.

entries.yeshivish_example: They put a heker on the table while eating together.
entries.plain_english_example: They placed a visible reminder on the table as required during niddah.
meanings: distinctive reminder used in specified niddah situations
entries.context_note: Commonly refers to a visible change or reminder used when a husband and wife eat together during niddah.

entries.yeshivish_example: The harchakos include restrictions on negiah.
entries.plain_english_example: The distancing rules include restrictions on physical touch.
entries.context_note: A broader halachic term also used outside marriage; in this category it refers to physical contact during niddah.

entries.yeshivish_example: The shiur discussed mitzvas onah.
entries.plain_english_example: The lesson discussed the marital-intimacy obligation in Jewish law.
entries.context_note: A marriage-law term distinct from onah as a day/night time period.

entries.yeshivish_example: The wedding may have the status of a chupas niddah.
entries.plain_english_example: The wedding may take place while the bride is in niddah status.
meanings: wedding occurring while the bride is niddah
entries.context_note: This creates specialized wedding and post-wedding halachic considerations.

entries.yeshivish_example: She called a yoetzet halacha with the question.
entries.plain_english_example: She consulted a woman certified to advise on family-purity halacha.
meanings: female halachic adviser trained in taharas hamishpacha
entries.context_note: A modern professional role associated especially with women's halachic questions in family purity and related health contexts.

entries.yeshivish_example: The halachos for a yoledes came up after the birth.
entries.plain_english_example: The family-purity laws for a woman during and after childbirth came up after the birth.
meanings: woman during or after childbirth in relevant halachic status
entries.context_note: Childbirth has specific niddah and postpartum implications beyond this glossary-level definition.

entries.yeshivish_example: The veset rules can differ for a me'uberes.
entries.plain_english_example: The menstrual-calendar rules can differ for a pregnant woman.
entries.context_note: In family-purity halacha, pregnancy can affect veset expectations and related rules.

entries.yeshivish_example: The status of a meinekes can affect veset calculations.
entries.plain_english_example: The status of a nursing or postpartum woman can affect menstrual-pattern calculations.
meanings: postpartum woman within a halachically defined nursing period
entries.context_note: Halachic usage can be broader than whether the woman is actively breastfeeding at that moment.

entries.yeshivish_example: She may have the status of mesulekes damim.
entries.plain_english_example: She may be in a category in which menstruation is not ordinarily expected.
meanings: woman not expected to menstruate in specified halachic circumstances
entries.context_note: A technical status used in veset law, including certain pregnancy, nursing, or later-life contexts.

entries.yeshivish_example: The laws discuss a zekeinah separately for some veset purposes.
entries.plain_english_example: The laws discuss an older woman separately for some menstrual-pattern purposes.
meanings: older woman in a technical niddah-law category
entries.context_note: The precise halachic definition is technical and should not be inferred merely from ordinary age terminology.

entries.yeshivish_example: The case raised a question of roah machmas tashmish.
entries.plain_english_example: The case raised the halachic category of uterine bleeding associated with marital relations.
meanings: uterine bleeding associated with marital relations in halachic terminology
entries.context_note: An advanced and medically sensitive halachic category requiring individualized rabbinic and often medical guidance.

entries.yeshivish_example: The Gemara distinguishes niddah from zivah.
entries.plain_english_example: The Talmud distinguishes menstrual bleeding from the classical category of non-menstrual uterine bleeding.
meanings: classical halachic category of non-menstrual uterine bleeding
entries.context_note: The classical Torah categories remain important in study even though modern practical niddah observance generally does not rely on women identifying these categories themselves.

entries.yeshivish_example: The sugya discusses the status of a zavah.
entries.plain_english_example: The Talmudic discussion addresses a woman in the classical zivah category.
meanings: woman with bleeding in the classical halachic category of zivah
entries.context_note: Primarily useful in Torah/Talmud study and the background of niddah law.

entries.yeshivish_example: The Mishnah discusses a zavah gedolah.
entries.plain_english_example: The Mishnah discusses the classical category associated with zivah bleeding on three consecutive days.
meanings: classical category of a zavah associated with three consecutive days of zivah bleeding
entries.context_note: Primarily a classical halachic-study term; modern practical application requires expert halachic framing.

entries.yeshivish_example: The sugya distinguishes a zavah ketanah from a zavah gedolah.
entries.plain_english_example: The Talmudic discussion distinguishes the shorter classical zivah category from the extended one.
meanings: classical category of a zavah associated with fewer than three consecutive days of zivah bleeding
entries.context_note: Primarily a classical halachic-study term; modern practical application requires expert halachic framing.
